  \[ \epsilon^*(\operatorname{ind}_{\epsilon(H)}^K(\lambda)) \ \cong \ \operatorname{ind}_{\epsilon^{-1}(\epsilon(H))}^G(\lambda\circ\epsilon|_H)\ = \ \operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi) \ \cong \ \epsilon^*(W) \]
  as $G$-representations, we conclude that $\operatorname{ind}_{\epsilon(H)}^K(\lambda)$ is $K$-isomorphic to $W$.
  So $[\epsilon(H),\lambda]$ is a  monomial structure on $W$, and it inflates
  to the given monomial structure $[H,\chi]$.
<!-- end eg-3 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:Phi_on_irrep}
  For every nontrivial irreducible unitary representation $V$ of a compact Lie group $G$,
  the relation
  \[ \Phi^G(b_{G,V})\ = \ \sum_{[H,\chi]\in \operatorname{mon}(V)}( 1-\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)^\sharp )\]
  holds in the ring $\Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
We start with the special case where $G$ is a closed subgroup of $U(m)$,
  and  $V=\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_G(\nu_m)$ is the restriction of the tautological representation.
  The proof of Proposition \ref{prop:double_coset}
  provides a  $U(m)$-equivariant homeomorphism
  from  $U(m)/(\Sigma_m\wr T)$ to
  the space ${\mathcal L}_m$ of sets $\ell=\{L_1,\dots,L_m\}$ of
  $m$ pairwise orthogonal 1-dimensional subspaces of ${\mathbb C}^m$,
  by taking the columns of a matrix, see \eqref{eq:coset2L_n}.
  Hence the induced map on $G$-fixed points
  \[    (U(m)/(\Sigma_m\wr T))^G \ \cong \ ({\mathcal L}_m)^G\]
  is a homeomorphism, too.
  
  An element $\ell$ of ${\mathcal L}_m$ is $G$-fixed precisely if
  $G$ permutes the $m$ lines in $\ell$. Since $G$ acts irreducibly
  on $\nu_m$, the action of $G$ on such a set $\ell\in({\mathcal L}_m)^G$ must be transitive.
  Hence the stabilizer $H$ of every element $L\in\ell$ has index $m$ in $G$. 
  We let $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$ be the character that encodes the $H$-action on $L$, i.e.,
  \[ h\cdot x \ = \ \chi(h)\cdot x \]
  for all $(h,x)\in H\times L$.
  We let $x\in L$ be any unit vector.
  Then the map 
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:pref_iso}
    V\ \xrightarrow{\ \cong \ }\  \operatorname{map}^H(G,\chi^*(\nu_1)) =  \operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi)\ , \quad
    v \ \longmapsto \ \{ g\mapsto \langle g\cdot v,x\rangle\}  
  \end{equation}
  is an isomorphism of $G$-representations,
  so $(H,\chi)$ is a monomial datum for $V$.
  If $L'$ is another element of $\ell$, 
  then $L'=g L$ for some $g\in G$, so the stabilizer of $L'$ is ${^g H}$, and $^g H$ acts on $L'$
  through the character $\chi\circ c_g$. So the $G$-conjugacy class
  of the monomial datum is independent of the choice of line in $\ell\in ({\mathcal L}_m)^G$.
  In other words, the map
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:map_back}
    ({\mathcal L}_m)^G\ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{mon}(V) \ , \quad \ell \ \longmapsto [H,\chi]
  \end{equation}
  is well-defined.

  Now we let $\ell$, $\ell'$ be two elements of $({\mathcal L}_m)^G$ such that $[H,\chi]=[H',\chi']$
  in $\operatorname{mon}(V)$. Then there are lines $L\in\ell$ and $L'\in \ell'$
  such that the associated monomial data $(H,\chi)$ and $(H',\chi')$ are $G$-conjugate.
  So after replacing $L'$ by a suitable $G$-translate, if necessary,
  we can assume that $L$ and $L'$ have the same stabilizer group $H$,
  and the $H$-action on $L$ and $L'$ is given by the same character $\chi$.
  After choosing unit vectors $x\in L$ and $x'\in L'$,
  each of them defines an isomorphism of $G$-representations \eqref{eq:pref_iso}.
  By direct inspection, these send $x$ and $x'$, respectively,
  to the distinguished function $\chi^\dagger\colon G\longrightarrow{\mathbb C}$ defined by
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:chi^dagger}
    \chi^\dagger(\gamma)\ = \
    \begin{cases}
      \chi(\gamma) & \text{ for $\gamma\in H$, and}\\
    \  0 & \text{ for $\gamma\not\in H$.}
    \end{cases}
   \end{equation}
  Since $V$ is irreducible, the two isomorphisms
  differ by multiplication by a scalar in $T$, so we must have $x'=\lambda x$
  for some $\lambda\in T$. In particular $L'={\mathbb C}\cdot x'={\mathbb C}\cdot x=L$.
  Hence also the $G$-orbits $\ell=G\cdot L$ and $\ell'=G\cdot L'$
  are equal in $({\mathcal L}_m)^G$. In other words, the map \eqref{eq:map_back}
  is injective.

  If $(H,\chi)$ is any monomial datum for $V$, then the induced representation
  $\operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi)$ comes with a preferred $G$-invariant set of pairwise orthogonal lines,
  namely the set
  \[ \{ {\mathbb C}\cdot g\cdot \chi^\dagger\}_{g\in G} \]
  of lines spanned by the $G$-translates of the distinguished function \eqref{eq:chi^dagger}.
  Moreover, $H$ is the stabilizer group of the line ${\mathbb C}\cdot \chi^\dagger$,
  and $H$ acts on this line by the character $\chi$.
  So the image of this set under any isomorphism of $G$-representations
  \[    \operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi)\ \cong \ V  \]
  is an element of $({\mathcal L}_m)^G$, and the image of ${\mathbb C}\cdot \chi^\dagger$
  is an element with stabilizer group $H$ and character $\chi$.
  So the map \eqref{eq:map_back} is surjective, and hence bijective.
  In sum, we have now established a bijection
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:fix2Ind}
    (U(m)/(\Sigma_m\wr T))^G \ \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ } \ \operatorname{mon}(V)
  \end{equation}
  that sends a $G$-fixed coset $A\cdot(\Sigma_m\wr T)$ to the
  monomial structure $[H,\chi]$, where
  $H$ is the stabilizer group of the line ${\mathbb C}\cdot A\cdot e_1$,
  and $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$ encodes the $H$-action on this line.
  
  Now we prove the claim in the special case.
  Proposition 3.4.2 (ii) of \cite{schwede:global} shows that
  \[ \Phi^G\circ \operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_G\circ \operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}\ = \ \sum_{A(\Sigma_m\wr T)\in (U(m)/(\Sigma_m\wr T))^G} \Phi^G\circ A_\star\circ \operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}_{G^A}\ . \]
  Here $G^A=A^{-1} G A$, and $A_\star$ is restriction along the conjugation
  homomorphism $c_A\colon G\longrightarrow G^A$.
  We have used that the space $(U(m)/(\Sigma_m\wr T))^G$
  is finite by the bijection \eqref{eq:fix2Ind}
  and the finiteness of $\operatorname{mon}(V)$, so that its path components
  are points and have Euler characteristic equal to 1. Then
  \begin{align*}
    \Phi^G(b_{G,V})\
    &= \ \Phi^G(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_G(b_m))\ = \ \Phi^G(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_G(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}(P^m(b_1))))\\
    &=\  \sum_{A (\Sigma_m\wr T)\in  (U(m)/(\Sigma_m\wr T))^G}
      \Phi^G(A_\star(\operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}_{G^A}(P^m(b_1))))\ .
  \end{align*}
  We use the bijection \eqref{eq:fix2Ind} to replace the indexing set
  of the sum by the set of monomial structures on $V$,
  and we rewrite the corresponding summand.

  Given any $G$-fixed point $A (\Sigma_m\wr T)\in  (U(m)/(\Sigma_m\wr T))^G$,
  we set $v_i=A\cdot e_i$, where $e_i$ is the $i$th vector of the standard basis
  of ${\mathbb C}^m$. Then $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ is a monomial basis for $V$, i.e.,
  an orthonormal basis in which the $G$-action is given entirely
  by monomial matrices in $\Sigma_m\wr T$.
  We let $H$ be the stabilizer group of the line ${\mathbb C}\cdot v_1$,
  and we let $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$ encode the $H$-action on this line,
  so that $[H,\chi]$ is the monomial structure corresponding to
  $A (\Sigma_m\wr T)$ under the bijection \eqref{eq:fix2Ind}.
  
  Because $G$ acts irreducibly on $V$,
  it acts transitively on the set of lines $\{{\mathbb C}\cdot v_1,\dots,{\mathbb C}\cdot v_m\}$.
  So we can choose an $H$-transversal $\bar g=(g_1,\dots,g_m)$ such that
  $g_i\cdot v_1=\lambda_i\cdot v_i$ for some $\lambda_i\in T$.
  The matrix $B=A\cdot(1;\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m)$ is then another representative
  of the same coset $A (\Sigma_m\wr T)=B (\Sigma_m\wr T)$.
  Moreover, $B \cdot e_i=A \cdot \lambda_i\cdot e_i=\lambda_i\cdot v_i$.
  We claim that  the following diagram commutes:
  \[ \xymatrix{ G \ar[r]^-{\Psi_{\bar g}}\ar[d]_{c_B} & \Sigma_m\wr H\ar[d]^{\Sigma_m\wr\chi} \\
      G^B\ar[r]_-{\text{incl}} & \Sigma_m\wr T } \]
  To this end we consider $\gamma\in G$ and set $\Psi_{\bar g}(\gamma)=(\sigma;h_1,\dots,h_m)$,
  which means that
  \[ \gamma\cdot g_i \ = \ g_{\sigma(i)}\cdot h_i \]
  for all $1\leq i\leq m$. Then
  \begin{align*}
    c_B(\gamma)\cdot e_i\
    &= \ B^{-1}\cdot\gamma\cdot B \cdot e_i\ = \ B^{-1} \cdot \gamma\cdot \lambda_i\cdot v_i\
    = \  B^{-1} \cdot \gamma\cdot g_i\cdot v_1\\
    &= \  B^{-1} \cdot g_{\sigma(i)}\cdot h_i\cdot v_1\
    = \  B^{-1} \cdot g_{\sigma(i)}\cdot \chi(h_i)\cdot v_1\
    = \ \chi(h_i)\cdot  B^{-1} \cdot \lambda_{\sigma(i)}\cdot v_{\sigma(i)}\\
    &= \ \chi(h_i)\cdot  e_{\sigma(i)}\ =\
      (\sigma;\chi(h_1),\dots,\chi(h_m))\cdot e_i\ = \ (\Sigma_m\wr \chi)(\Psi_{\bar g}(\gamma))\cdot e_i\ ,
  \end{align*}
  also for all $1\leq i\leq m$. Since the matrices $c_B(\gamma)$
  and $((\Sigma_m\wr \chi)\circ\Psi_{\bar g})(\gamma)$ have the same effect on a basis of ${\mathbb C}^m$,
  they agree.
  The commutative square then yields
  \begin{align*}
    \Phi^G(B_\star(\operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}_{G^B}(P^m(b_1))))\
    &= \ \Phi^G( \Psi_{\bar g}^*((\Sigma_m\wr \chi)^*(P^m(b_1))))\\
    &= \ \Phi^G( \Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(\chi^*(b_1))))\
    = \ \Phi^G( \Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(b_{H,\chi})))\ = \  1- \operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)^\sharp\ .
  \end{align*}
  The second equation is the naturality of power operations
  for restriction along continuous homomorphisms.
  The final equation is Proposition \ref{prop:monomial_basis} (iv);
  we use here that $\chi$ is nontrivial because $V$ is nontrivial irreducible.
  This completes the proof in the special case.
  
  Now we consider a general nontrivial and irreducible $G$-representation $V$.
  It is isomorphic to $\alpha^*(\nu_m)$
  for some continuous homomorphism $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow U(m)$,
  so we may assume that $V=\alpha^*(\nu_m)$.
  We let $K=\alpha(G)$ be the image of $\alpha$, a closed subgroup of $U(m)$.
  We let $\epsilon\colon G\longrightarrow K$ be the continuous epimorphism given by $\alpha$,
  with restricted codomain.
  Then $\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_K(\nu_m)$ is nontrivial irreducible, and the special case applies to it.
  As we explained in Example \ref{eg:inflate_mon}, the inflation map \eqref{eq:inflate_mon}
  that sends a monomial structure $[L,\lambda]$ on $\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_K(\nu_m)$
  to the monomial structure $[\epsilon^{-1}(L),\lambda\circ \epsilon|_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)}]$
  on $\epsilon^*(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_K(\nu_m))=V$ is bijective.
  Transfers commute with inflation, in the sense that
  \[ \epsilon^*(\operatorname{tr}_L^K(\lambda)) \ = \
    \operatorname{tr}_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)}^G(\epsilon^*(\lambda)) \ = \
    \operatorname{tr}_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)}^G(\lambda\circ\epsilon|_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)}) \ .
  \]
 Hence
  \begin{align*}
    \Phi^G(b_{G,V})\
    &= \ \Phi^G(\epsilon^*(b_{K,\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_K(\nu_m)})) 
      \ = \ \epsilon^*(\Phi^K(b_{K,\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_K(\nu_m)})) \\
    &= \  \sum_{[L,\lambda]\in\operatorname{mon}(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_K(\nu_m))} ( 1-\epsilon^*(\operatorname{tr}_L^K(\lambda)^\sharp ))\\
    &= \  \sum_{[L,\lambda]\in\operatorname{mon}(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_K(\nu_m))} ( 1-\operatorname{tr}_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)}^G(\lambda\circ \epsilon|_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)})^\sharp )\
    = \  \sum_{[H,\chi]\in\operatorname{mon}(V)} ( 1-\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)^\sharp )\ .
  \end{align*}
  So the theorem holds for the $G$-representation $V$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- eg-4: body_md -->
\label{eg:several_monomial_structures}
  An irreducible $G$-representation can have several monomial structures,
  so the right hand side of the formula in Theorem \ref{thm:Phi_on_irrep}
  may have more than one summand.
  An example is the quaternion group $G=Q=\{\pm 1,\pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$,
  with $i^2=j^2=k^2=i j k=-1$.
  The group $Q$ has four 1-dimensional representations,
  and one other irreducible representation of dimension 2.
  The cyclic subgroups
  $I=\{\pm 1,\pm i\}$, $J=\{\pm 1,\pm j\}$ and $K=\{\pm 1,\pm k\}$
  of order~4 are normal in $Q$, but they are not conjugate.
  We let $\alpha\colon I\longrightarrow T$,
  $\beta\colon J\longrightarrow T$ and $\gamma\colon K\longrightarrow T$  be any monomorphisms.
  Then the induced 2-dimensional representations
  $\operatorname{ind}_I^Q(\alpha)$, $\operatorname{ind}_J^Q(\beta)$ and $\operatorname{ind}_K^Q(\gamma)$
  are irreducible, and hence isomorphic.
  So $[I,\alpha]$, $[J,\beta]$ and $[K,\gamma]$ are three distinct
  monomial structures on the 2-dimensional irreducible $Q$-representation,
  and in fact all such monomial structures.
<!-- end eg-4 -->
<!-- defn-5: body_md -->
\label{def:near-cyclic}
  A finite group $G$ is {\em near-cyclic} if it is not cyclic,
  and for every normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ with $N\ne\{1\}$,
  the quotient group $G/N$ is cyclic.
<!-- end defn-5 -->
<!-- prop-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:nearcyclic}
  Every finite near-cyclic group $G$ has exactly one of the following three properties.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (a)]
  \item The group $G$ is an elementary abelian $p$-group of rank~2, for some prime $p$.
  \item The commutator subgroup $G'=[G,G]$ is nontrivial and abelian,
    and the conjugation action of the abelianization $G_{\operatorname{ab}}=G/G'$
    on $G'\setminus\{1\}$ is free.
  \item The commutator subgroup $G'$ is nontrivial and perfect.
    In particular, $G$ is not solvable.
  \end{enumerate}
  Moreover, if $G$ has property {\em (b)} or {\em (c)},
  then there is a subgroup $H$ of $G$ and a nontrivial character $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$
  such that $\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)=1$.
<!-- end prop-10 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
If $G$ is abelian and not cyclic, then it admits an epimorphism
  onto $C_p\times C_p$, for some prime $p$. So if $G$ is abelian and near-cyclic,
  it belongs to class (a).

  Now we suppose that $G$ is nonabelian, i.e., its commutator subgroup $G'$ is nontrivial.
  If the commutator subgroup is perfect, then $G$ belongs to class (c).
  We let $H$ be a nontrivial cyclic subgroup of $G'$, and we let $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$
  be any nontrivial character. Since $G'$ is perfect, every $G'$-character is trivial,
  so in particular $\operatorname{tr}_H^{G'}(\chi)=1$. Transitivity of transfers then yields
  \[ \operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)\ = \ \operatorname{tr}_{G'}^G(\operatorname{tr}_H^{G'}(\chi))\ = \ \operatorname{tr}_{G'}^G(1)\ = \ 1 \ .  \]
  
  For the rest of the argument we assume that $G$ is near-cyclic, nonabelian
  and the commutator subgroup $G'$ is not perfect.
  We will argue in several steps that then $G$ has property (b).
  Since the commutator subgroup $G'$ is nontrivial and normal,
  and since $G$ is near-cyclic, the abelianization $G_{\operatorname{ab}}=G/G'$ is cyclic.
  The iterated commutator subgroup $G''=[G',G']$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
  Since $G'$ is not perfect, $G''$ is strictly contained in $G'$. So $G/G''$ is
  a nonabelian quotient of $G$. Since $G$ is near-cyclic, $G''$ must be trivial,
  i.e., $G'$ is abelian. 

  Now we show that the center $Z(G)$ of $G$ is trivial.
  Otherwise, $G/Z(G)$ would be cyclic, by near-cyclicity of $G$.
  Then $G$ is generated by $Z(G)$ and any lift of a generator of $G/Z(G)$;
  since these elements commute with themselves and each other, $G$ would be abelian,
  contradicting the hypothesis.
  
  Now we show that $G$ belongs to class (b).
  For any element $g\in G\setminus G'$, we consider
  the centralizer of $g$ inside the commutator subgroup $G'$,
  \[ N\ =\ C_{G'}(g)\ = \ C_G(g)\cap G'\ . \]
  We show that $N$ is normal in $G$.
  Since $G'$  is abelian and normal, the conjugation action of 
  $G$ on $G'$ factors through $G_{\operatorname{ab}}=G/G'$, making 
  $G'$  a ${\mathbb Z}[G_{\operatorname{ab}}]$-module. For any 
  $g\in G$ with image $\bar g=g G'$ in $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$, we have 
  $N=C_{G'}(g)=\{a\in G'\colon {^{\bar g} a}=a\}$, i.e., 
  $N$ is the fixed subgroup of $\bar g$ acting on 
  $G'$. Since $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ is cyclic, hence abelian, $\bar g$
  commutes with every element of $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$, so the fixed-point subgroup 
  $N$ is $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$-invariant, and hence normal in $G$, as claimed.
  
  Now we show that $N$ is strictly smaller than $G'$.
  To prove that we argue by contradiction.
  If $N=G'$, then $g$ would centralize $G'$.
  We let $t\in G$ be an element whose coset $t G'\in G/G'=G_{\operatorname{ab}}$
  generates the abelianization.
  We write $g=t^i\cdot \gamma$ for some $i\geq 0$ and some $\gamma\in G'$.
  Because $G'$ is abelian, $\gamma$ centralizes $G'$.
  Hence $t^i=g\gamma^{-1}$ centralizes $G'$. Since $t^i$ also commutes with $t$,
  the element $t^i$ is central in $G$. Since $G$ is centerless,
  we conclude that $t^i=1$, and thus $g=\gamma\in G'$, contradicting the hypothesis on $g$.
  This proves that $N$ is a proper subgroup of $G'$.
  So $G/N$ is a nonabelian quotient of $G$.
  Since $G$ is near-cyclic, we must have $N=\{1\}$.
  So conjugation by $g$ does not fix any element of $G'\setminus\{1\}$,
  i.e., $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ acts freely on $G'\setminus\{1\}$. So $G$ belongs to class (b).

  Since $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ acts freely on $G'\setminus\{1\}$,
  the order of $G'$ is congruent to 1 modulo the order of $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$;
  in particular, the orders of $G'$ and $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ are coprime.
  We let $\chi\colon G'\longrightarrow T$ be any nontrivial character,
  which exists because $G'$ is abelian and nontrivial.
  The transfer $\operatorname{tr}_{G'}^G\colon\operatorname{Hom}(G',T)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(G,T)$
  is a group homomorphism; its source has the same order as $G'$,
  and its target has the same order as $\operatorname{Hom}(G_{\operatorname{ab}},T)$, and hence as $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$.
  Since the orders of $G'$ and $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ are coprime, this transfer homomorphism
  must be trivial. Hence $\operatorname{tr}_{G'}^G(\chi)=1$, and the addendum holds for $H=G'$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:rep_with_trivial_Phi-finite}
  Let $G$ be a non-cyclic finite group.
  Then there is a unitary $G$-representation $V$ with $V^G=0$
  such that $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$ in $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
We start with the case where $G$ is near-cyclic.
  Then $G$ has one of the three properties (a), (b) or (c)
  specified in Proposition \ref{prop:nearcyclic}. We give separate constructions
  of the desired $G$-representation.

  (a) For $G=C_p\times C_p$ for some prime $p$,
  we can let $V$ be the reduced regular representation,
  which is isomorphic to the direct sum of all nontrivial
  irreducible $G$-representations;
  hence 
  \[ b_{G,V}\ =\  \prod_{\chi\ne 1} b_{C_p\times C_p,\chi}\ , \]
  where the product is over all nontrivial homomorphisms $\chi\colon C_p\times C_p\longrightarrow T$.
  The relation
  \[ \prod_{\chi\ne 1} ( 1-\chi)\  =\  0\]
  holds in the group ring ${\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(C_p\times C_p,T)]$. 
  Multiplicativity of the pre-Bott classes then yields
  \[ \Phi^{C_p\times C_p}(b_{C_p\times C_p,V})\ = \
    \prod_{\chi\ne 1} \Phi^{C_p\times C_p}(b_{C_p\times C_p,\chi})\ =_{\eqref{eq:Phi^G_of_char}} \
    \prod_{\chi\ne 1} (1-\chi^\sharp)\ = \  0 \ . \]

  (b) We suppose that $G$ is nonabelian, the commutator subgroup $G'$ is abelian,
  and the conjugation action of $G_{\operatorname{ab}}=G/G'$ on $G'\setminus\{1\}$ is free.
  In this case the order of the commutator subgroup $G'$
  is congruent to 1 modulo the order of $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$,
  so the orders of $G'$ and $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ are coprime.
  Because $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ acts freely on $G'\setminus\{1\}$, it also acts freely
  on the set of nontrivial homomorphisms from $G'$ to $T$.
  We let $\chi\colon G'\longrightarrow T$ be any nontrivial homomorphism.
  Then $\chi\circ c_g\ne \chi$ for all $g\in G\setminus G'$.
  The induced $G$-representation $\operatorname{ind}_{G'}^G(\chi)$ is thus irreducible.
  The transfer $\operatorname{tr}_{G'}^G\colon\operatorname{Hom}(G',T)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(G,T)$
  is a group homomorphism; its source has the same order as $G'$,
  and its target has the same order as $\operatorname{Hom}(G_{\operatorname{ab}},T)$, and hence as $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$.
  Since the orders of $G'$ and $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ are coprime, this transfer homomorphism
  must be trivial. In particular, $\operatorname{tr}_{G'}^G(\chi)=1$.
  
  Since the orders of $G'$ and $G_{\operatorname{ab}}=G/G'$ are coprime, $G'$ is the only
  subgroup of $G$ of index $[G:G']$.
  So $[G',\chi]$ is the only monomial structure on $\operatorname{ind}_{G'}^G(\chi)$,
  by Proposition \ref{prop:unique_mon}.
  Hence for $V=\operatorname{ind}_{G'}^G(\chi)$, the formula of Theorem \ref{thm:Phi_on_irrep}
  has only one summand, and it yields the relation
  \[ \Phi^G(b_{G,V})\ = \  1-\operatorname{tr}_{G'}^G(\chi)^\sharp \ = 0 \ . \]

  (c) If $G$ is not solvable, then $G$ cannot be a monomial group,
  see  \cite{taketa:monomial} or \cite[Corollary 5.13]{isaacs:character}.
  Hence $G$ has an irreducible representation $V$ that is not
  induced from a 1-dimensional representation of any subgroup of $G$.
  Then $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$ by Theorem \ref{thm:Phi_on_irrep}.

  It remains to treat the case of a general non-cyclic finite group.
  Any non-cyclic group $G$ admits an epimorphism $\epsilon\colon G\longrightarrow K$
  onto a near-cyclic group. By the above, there is a $K$-representation $W$
  with $W^K=0$ and such that $\Phi^K(b_{K,W})=0$.
  Then $V=\epsilon^*(W)$ is the desired $G$-representation, because
  the geometric fixed point homomorphisms commute with inflation, see \eqref{eq:infl_and_fix-ROG},
  and thus
 \[   \Phi^G(b_{G,V})\ = \ \Phi^G( \epsilon^*(b_{K,W}))\
   =  \  \epsilon^*(\Phi^K(b_{K,W}))\ =\ 0 \ .\qedhere \]
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:G^circ_image}
  Let $G$ be a nonabelian compact Lie group whose identity component $G^\circ$ is abelian,
  and whose component group $\pi_0(G)$ is cyclic.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item 
    There is a unitary $G$-representation $V$ with $V^G=0$ such that
    $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$ in $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
  \item  There is a finite index subgroup $H$ of $G$ and
    a nontrivial continuous homomorphism $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$
    such that $\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
We first show a reduction scheme for epimorphisms.
  Let $\epsilon\colon K\longrightarrow G$ be a continuous epimorphism, and suppose that the
  conclusion of the theorem holds for $G$. Then the conclusion of
  the theorem also holds for $K$.
  Indeed, if $V$ is a unitary $G$-representation with $V^G=0$ and 
  $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$, the inflated $K$-representation $W=\epsilon^*(V)$
  satisfies $W^K=V^G=0$ and 
  \[ \Phi^K(b_{K,W})\ = \ \Phi^K(\epsilon^*(b_{G,V}))\ =_{\eqref{eq:infl_and_fix-ROG}} \
    \epsilon^*(\Phi^G(b_{G,V}))\ = \ 0\ . \]
  And if $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$ is a nontrivial continuous homomorphism from a
  finite index subgroup of $G$   
  such that $\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)=1$, then $L=\epsilon^{-1}(H)$
  is a finite index subgroup of $K$ and  $\beta=\chi\circ \epsilon|_L\colon L\longrightarrow T$
  is a nontrivial continuous homomorphism
  such that
  \[ \operatorname{tr}_L^K(\beta)\ = \ \operatorname{tr}_L^K(\epsilon|_L^*(\chi))\ = \
    \epsilon^*(\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi))\ = \ 1\ .\]  
  So whenever properties (i) and  (ii) hold for $G$, they also hold for $K$.

  Now we prove the theorem in three steps, for successively more general classes of groups.
  In the proof of the following first case, we shall need an algebraic fact.
  We let $A$ be a torsion-free abelian group
  equipped with a faithful action of a finite cyclic group $C$ of order $n$.
  Such an action has a free orbit, i.e., there is an element $a\in A$
  whose orbit $C a$ has $n$ elements.
  Now let $\tau\colon A\longrightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of abelian groups that is $C$-equivariant
  for the trivial $C$-action on the target.
  We define $b\in A$ by
  \[ b\ = \ n\cdot a - (a + t a +\dots + t^{n-1} a)\ ,\]
  where $t$ is a generator of $C$.
  Then $b$ lies in the kernel of $\tau$,
  and the $C$-orbit of $b$ also has $n$ elements.
  Indeed, if $t^k b = b$ for some $0 < k < n$,
  then expanding gives $n(t^k a - a) = 0$, so $t^k a = a$
  by torsion-freeness, contradicting the freeness of the orbit $C a$.
  So the kernel of $\tau$ contains a free $C$-orbit.
  
  Case 1: The conjugation action of $\pi_0(G)$ on $G^\circ$ is faithful.
  Then also the induced $\pi_0(G)$-action on $\operatorname{Hom}(G^\circ,T)$ is faithful.
  Since $G^\circ$ is a torus, the abelian group $\operatorname{Hom}(G^\circ,T)$ is torsion-free.
  Each element of $\pi_0(G)$ acts on $G^\circ$ by the restriction of an 
  inner automorphism of $G$. So the transfer homomorphism 
  \[ \operatorname{tr}_{G^\circ}^G \ \colon \ \operatorname{Hom}(G^\circ,T)\ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{Hom}(G,T) \]
  is equivariant for the trivial $\pi_0(G)$-action on the target.
  Since the $\pi_0(G)$-action on $\operatorname{Hom}(G^\circ,T)$ is faithful, the kernel of this transfer
  homomorphism contains a free $\pi_0(G)$-orbit, by the comment above.
  In other words: there is 
  a continuous homomorphism $\chi\colon G^\circ\longrightarrow T$ such that
  $\operatorname{tr}_{G^\circ}^G(\chi)=1$ and such that
  $\chi\circ c_g\ne \chi$ for all $g\in G\setminus G^\circ$.
  In particular, condition (ii) holds for $H=G^\circ$.

  The fact that $\chi\circ c_g\ne \chi$ for all $g\in G\setminus G^\circ$
  means that the induced $G$-representation $\operatorname{ind}_{G^\circ}^G(\chi)$
  is irreducible.
  Since $G^\circ$ is the only subgroup of $G$ whose index equals $[G:G^\circ]$,
  $[G^\circ,\chi]$ is the only monomial structure on $\operatorname{ind}_{G^\circ}^G(\chi)$,
  by Proposition \ref{prop:unique_mon}.
  Theorem  \ref{thm:Phi_on_irrep} then lets us conclude
  \[ \Phi^G(b_{G,\operatorname{ind}_{G^\circ}^G(\chi)}) \ = \ 1 -\operatorname{tr}_{G^\circ}^G(\chi)^\sharp\ = \ 0\ .\]
  So condition (i) holds for $V=\operatorname{ind}_{G^\circ}^G(\chi)$.
  
  Case 2: The projection $q\colon G\longrightarrow G/G^\circ=\pi_0(G)$ has a multiplicative section.
  We can assume without loss of generality that $G=C\ltimes_\psi G^\circ$
  is the semidirect product of an action of a finite cyclic group $C$
  on a torus $G^\circ$, given by a homomorphism $\psi\colon C\longrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(G^\circ)$.
  We let $D$ be the kernel of $\psi$, i.e., the subgroup
  of $C$ consisting of the elements that act trivially on $G^\circ$.
  Then the $C$-action descends uniquely to a faithful action $\bar\psi\colon C/D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(G^\circ)$
  of the quotient group,
  and the group $G$ surjects onto the semidirect product $\bar G=(C/D)\ltimes_{\bar\psi}G^\circ$.
  Since $G$ is nonabelian, the $C$-action on $G^\circ$ is nontrivial.
  Hence also the induced $(C/D)$-action on $G^\circ$ is nontrivial,
  and the group $\bar G$ is nonabelian.
  Moreover the component group $\pi_0(\bar G)$ is isomorphic to $C/D$,
  hence cyclic, in a way that identifies the conjugation action
  on $\bar G^\circ=G^\circ$ with the action $\bar\psi\colon C/D\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(G^\circ)$.
  Since $C/D$ acts faithfully on $G^\circ$ by design, the group $\bar G$
  satisfies the hypothesis of case 1.
  Since the theorem holds for $\bar G$ by case 1,
  the epimorphic reduction scheme proves the theorem for the group $G$.

  Case 3, the general case:
  We let $N=Z(G)\cap G^\circ$ be the intersection of the center of $G$
  with the identity component $G^\circ$.
  We claim that the quotient group $G/N$ is nonabelian.
  If $G/N$ were abelian, then the commutator subgroup $G'$ of $G$ would
  be contained in $N$, and hence central in $G$. Since the abelianization $G_{\operatorname{ab}}=G/G'$
  has a cyclic component group $\pi_0(G_{\operatorname{ab}})=(\pi_0(G))_{\operatorname{ab}}=\pi_0(G)$,
  the abelianization is itself cyclic.
  But any group that has a central subgroup with cyclic quotient is abelian,
  contradicting the hypothesis on $G$. This shows that $G/N$ is nonabelian.
  The identity component of $G/N$ is $G^\circ/N$, and thus abelian.
  Since $N$ is contained in $G^\circ$, the quotient map $G\longrightarrow G/N$
  induces an isomorphism of component groups $\pi_0(G)\cong\pi_0(G/N)$.
  
  We claim that the projection $G/N\longrightarrow\pi_0(G/N)$ has a multiplicative section.
  To this end we let $t\in G$ be an element whose class $t\cdot G^\circ$ in $G/G^\circ=\pi_0(G)$
  generates the cyclic component group.
  Then the image of $t$ also generates the cyclic group $\pi_0(G/N)$.
  If $n=[G:G^\circ]$ is the order of $\pi_0(G)$, and hence also of $\pi_0(G/N)$,
  then $t^n\in G^\circ$.
  Since $G^\circ$ is abelian, $t^n$ commutes with $t$ and with $G^\circ$.
  Since $G$ is generated by $t$ and $G^\circ$, the element $t^n$ is central,
  and thus $t^n\in N$.
  So the quotient map $G/N\longrightarrow \pi_0(G/N)$
  has a multiplicative section, as claimed.
  Since the theorem holds for $G/N$ by case 2,
  the epimorphic reduction scheme proves the theorem for the group $G$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:rep_with_trivial_Phi-Lie}
  Let $G$ be a non-cyclic compact Lie group.
  Then there is a unitary $G$-representation $V$ with $V^G=0$ such that
  $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$ in $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
We distinguish three cases.
  
  (a) If the component group $\pi_0(G)$ is not cyclic,
  then Theorem \ref{thm:rep_with_trivial_Phi-finite}
  provides a $\pi_0(G)$-representation $W$ such that
  $W^{\pi_0(G)}=0$ and $\Phi^{\pi_0(G)}(b_{\pi_0(G),W})=0$.
  We let $q\colon G\longrightarrow G/G^\circ=\pi_0(G)$ denote the projection.
  Then the inflation $q^*(W)$ has the desired property, because
   $(q^*(W))^G=W^{\pi_0(G)}=0$ and
  \[   \Phi^G( b_{G,q^*(W)})\ = \  \Phi^G( q^*(b_{\pi_0(G),W}))\
    =  \  q^*(\Phi^{\pi_0(G)}(b_{\pi_0(G),W}))\ =\ 0 \ .\]
  
  (b) If the identity component $G^\circ$ is nonabelian,
  then $G^\circ$ has irreducible representations
  of arbitrarily large dimensions, see for example
  \cite[Chapter VI, (1.20), Exercise 2]{broecker-tomdieck}.
  Since every irreducible $G^\circ$-representation is a
  $G^\circ$-equivariant summand of some irreducible $G$-representation,
  $G$ itself has irreducible representations of arbitrarily large dimensions.
  In particular, there is an irreducible $G$-representation $V$ whose dimension exceeds
  the cardinality of the finite group $\pi_0(G)$.
  Then $G$ has no closed subgroup of finite index equal to the dimension of $V$,
  so $V$ has no monomial structure.
  Hence $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$ by Theorem \ref{thm:Phi_on_irrep}.
  
  (c) If the component group $\pi_0(G)$ is cyclic
  and the identity component $G^\circ$ is abelian,
  then $G$ itself must be nonabelian, for otherwise it would be cyclic.
  So Theorem \ref{thm:G^circ_image} (i) provides the desired $G$-representation.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- construction-8: body_md -->
The morphism of non-equivariant spectra from $\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty$ to $K U$ 
  that classifies the tautological complex line bundle over ${\mathbb C} P^\infty$
  has a particularly nice and prominent global-equivariant refinement,
  a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra:
  \[ \eta\  : \ \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}\ \longrightarrow\ {\mathbf{KU}}\ . \]
  The morphism is defined 
  as a composite of two morphisms of ultra-commutative ring spectra
  \[ \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}\ \xrightarrow{\ \mu\ }\  {\mathbf{ku}}\ \xrightarrow{\ j \ }\ {\mathbf{KU}} \ .\]
  The intermediate object is
  the connective global $K$-theory spectrum \cite[Construction 6.3.9]{schwede:global},
  and the first morphism $\mu$ is the inclusion of the `rank 1' part
  in the rank filtration, compare \cite[Construction 6.3.40]{schwede:global}.
  The second morphism $j$ is a `periodization morphism' $j\colon {\mathbf{ku}}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$
  defined in \cite[Construction 6.4.13]{schwede:global}.


  The underlying morphism of global spectra classifies
  the tautological $T$-representation on ${\mathbb C}$, in the following sense.
  As mentioned earlier, ${\mathbf P}$ is a global classifying space for the group $T$,
  so the pair $(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P},e_T)$  represents the functor $\pi_0^T$,
  where $e_T \in  \pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  is the stable tautological class \eqref{eq:define_e_T}.
  Under the preferred identification \cite[Theorem 6.4.24]{schwede:global}
  of $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})$ with the complex representation ring $RU(T)$, 
  the element $e_T$ maps to the class of the
  tautological $T$-representation on ${\mathbb C}$, i.e.,
  \[ \eta_*(e_T)\ = \ [\nu_1] \quad \text{in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})\cong RU(T)$.} \]
  Because $\eta$ is a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra,
  its effect on equivariant homotopy groups is not only compatible with restrictions,
  inflations and transfers, but also with multiplicative power operations and norms.
<!-- end construction-8 -->
<!-- rk-5: body_md -->
\label{rk:preBott2Bott}
  We will show in Theorem \ref{thm:pre-Bott} below
  that any morphism $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$ of commutative global ring spectra
  satisfying $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$  inverts all the pre-Bott classes $b_m$.
  An invertible class in the same representation-grading as $\eta_*(b_m)$
  is the $U(m)$-equivariant Bott class, also called the {\em Thom class},
  of the tautological $U(m)$-representation $\nu_m$.
  More generally, the equivariant Bott class of a unitary $G$-representation $V$
  is defined for example
  by Atiyah \cite[Section 4]{atiyah:elliptic},
  Segal \cite[\S 3]{segal:equivariant K-theory},
  or Karoubi \cite[Section III]{karoubi:sur la K-theorie}.  
  We write $\beta_{G,V}\in  \pi_V^G({\mathbf{KU}})$
  for the image of this Bott class under the isomorphism
  \[  \widetilde{KU}_G(S^V)  \ \xrightarrow{\ \cong \ } \ \widetilde{{\mathbf{KU}}}_G^0(S^V)  =  \pi_V^G({\mathbf{KU}})      \]
  established in \cite[Corollary 6.4.23]{schwede:global}.
  We claim that $\eta_*(b_{G,V})=\beta_{G,V}$.
  
  We start with the case $G=T$ and $V=\nu_1$.
  The $T$-equivariant Bott class of $\nu_1$ is in essence defined as the reduced
  $K$-theory class of the tautological $T$-equivariant line bundle
  over $P({\mathbb C}\oplus\nu_1)$, pulled back along a specific equivariant
  homeomorphism to $S^{\nu_1}$. All we need to know in the following is that
  it restricts to the classical non-equivariant Bott class,
  and that its image under
  $i^*\colon\widetilde{KU}_T(S^{\nu_1})\longrightarrow  \widetilde{KU}_T(S^0)= RU(T)$
  is the class $1-[\nu_1]$. Since the isomorphisms of
  \cite[Corollary 6.4.23]{schwede:global} are natural for equivariant maps,
  and compatible with $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})=RU(T)$, also  $i^*(\beta_{T,\nu_1})=1-[\nu_1]$.
  Moreover
  \[ i^*(\eta_*(b_1))\ = \ \eta_*(i^*(b_1)) \ = \ \eta_*(1-e_T)\ = \  1-[\nu_1] \ .\]
  Like for any global spectrum, the restriction homomorphism
  $i^*\colon \pi_{\nu_1}^T({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})$ is injective,
  compare the short exact sequence in Remark \ref{rk:b_1_unique},
  which proves that $\eta_*(b_1)=\beta_{T,\nu_1}$.

  The equivariant Bott classes are multiplicative and natural for restriction.
  For $m\geq 2$, this yields
  \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}(\eta_*(b_m))\
    &= \  \eta_*(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}(b_m))\
      = \  \eta_*(b_1\times\dots\times b_1)\\
    &= \  \eta_*(b_1)\times\dots\times\eta_*(b_1)\ = \
      \beta_{T,\nu_1}\times\dots\times\beta_{T,\nu_1}\\ 
    &= \  \beta_{T^m,\nu_1^m}\ =\ \operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}(\beta_{U(m),\nu_m})\ .
  \end{align*}
  The second equation is Theorem \ref{thm:fix of pre-Bott} (i). 
  Because the restriction map of representation rings $\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}\colon RU(U(m))\longrightarrow RU(T^m)$
  is injective, so is the restriction map
  $\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}\colon \pi_{\nu_m}^{U(m)}({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow\pi_{\nu_1^m}^{T^m}({\mathbf{KU}})$,
  by Bott periodicity for unitary representations in equivariant $K$-theory.
  Hence the previous relation implies that $\eta_*(b_m)=\beta_{U(m),\nu_m}$.
  A general unitary representation is isomorphic to $\alpha^*(\nu_m)$
  for some continuous homomorphism $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow U(m)$.
  Since the pre-Bott classes and the equivariant Bott classes
  are all natural for restriction along continuous homomorphisms,
  the relation $\eta_*(b_{G,V})=\beta_{G,V}$ follows.
<!-- end rk-5 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:pre-Bott}
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ be a morphism of commutative global ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})=RU(T)$.
    Then $\eta$ inverts the  pre-Bott classes $b_m$ for all $m\geq 1$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
We start with the case $m=1$, showing that $\eta_*(b_1)$ is invertible.
  We use that $\eta_*(b_1)$ equals the equivariant
  Bott class $\beta=\beta_{T,\nu_1}$, see Remark \ref{rk:preBott2Bott}.
  While the Thom isomorphism says that exterior multiplication by $\beta$
  is an isomorphism of reduced equivariant $K$-groups, this is not quite
  the same statement as invertibility in the sense of Definition \ref{def:RO-invertible},
  so we need an extra argument.
  The right square in the following diagram
  commutes because $\beta^\flat\colon{\mathbf{KU}}\wedge S^{\nu_1}\longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ is a morphism of $T$-spectra:
  \[ \xymatrix@C=12mm{
      0\ar[r] & \pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})\ar[r]^-{({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge i)_*}\ar@{=}[d] &  \pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge S^{\nu_1})\ar[r]^-{\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}} \ar[d]^{\beta^\flat_*} &
      \pi_0({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge S^2) \ar[d]^{\beta^\flat_*} \ar[r]& 0\\
      0\ar[r] &\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})\ar[r]_-{(1-[\nu_1])\cdot -} &    \pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})\ar[r]_-{\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}} &
      \pi_0({\mathbf{KU}})\ar[r] & 0 
    } \]
  The left square commutes because
  \[ \beta^\flat_*(({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge i)_*(x)) \ = \  i^*(\beta)\cdot x \ = \ (1-[\nu_1])\cdot x\]
  for all $x\in\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})$.
  We claim that both rows are exact.
  The upper row is part of the long exact homology sequence of
  the cofiber sequence of based $T$-spaces \eqref{eq:Tcof}, combined with
  the Wirthm{\"u}ller isomorphism $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge T_+\wedge S^1)\cong\pi_0({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge S^2)$.
  It is short exact because the adjacent terms are non-equivariant and $T$-equivariant
  homotopy groups of ${\mathbf{KU}}$ of odd degrees, and thus trivial.
  The lower row is exact because $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})$
  is a Laurent polynomial ring on the class $[\nu_1]$, and hence a domain
  whose augmentation ideal is generated by $1-[\nu_1]$.
  
  The $T$-equivariant Bott class restricts
  to the classical non-equivariant Bott class in $\pi_2({\mathbf{KU}})$,
  which is invertible in the graded ring $\pi_*({\mathbf{KU}})$;
  in the model for complex $K$-theory that we work with, this is
  proved in \cite[Theorem 6.4.29]{schwede:global}.
  So the right vertical map in the above commutative diagram is bijective.
  The middle vertical map is thus bijective by the five lemma.
  In particular, there is a class $u\in\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge S^{\nu_1})$
  such that $\beta^\flat_*(u)=1$, and so the class $\beta=\eta_*(b_1)$
  is invertible by Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion}.

  Now we consider $m\geq 2$.
  Since the class $\eta_*(b_1)=\beta$ is invertible, so is its
  power $P^m(\beta)$, by Proposition \ref{prop:invertibility_power}.
  We let $\lambda\in \pi_0^{\Sigma_m\wr T}({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge S^{\nu_1^m})$ be the inverse of $P^m(\beta)$,
  i.e., the unique class such that $(P^m(\beta))^\flat_*(\lambda)=1$.
  We claim that
  \[ \operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}(\lambda) \ \in \ \pi_0^{U(m)}({\mathbf{KU}}\wedge S^{\nu_m})\]
  is inverse to $\eta_*(b_m)$.
  To this end we calculate
  \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}((\eta_*(b_m))^\flat_*(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}(\lambda)))\
    &= \   (\eta_*(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}(b_m)))^\flat_*(\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}(\lambda)))\\
    &= \   (\eta_*(b_1\times\dots\times b_1))^\flat_*(\operatorname{res}_{T^m}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}(\lambda))\\
  &= \   (\beta\times\dots\times\beta)^\flat_*(\operatorname{res}_{T^m}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}(\lambda))\\
    &= \   \operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}_{T^m}( (P^m(\beta))^\flat_*(\lambda))\
      = \   \operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}_{T^m}(1)\ =\ 1\ .
  \end{align*}
  The second equation uses Theorem \ref{thm:fix of pre-Bott} (i) and the double coset formula
  $\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}\circ \operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}=\operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_m\wr T}_{T^m}$, compare
  \cite[IV Corollary 6.7 (i)]{lms}.
  
  The restriction homomorphism $\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}\colon \pi_0^{U(m)}({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow
  \pi_0^{T^m}({\mathbf{KU}})$ is isomorphic to the
  restriction homomorphism of representation rings $\operatorname{res}^{U(m)}_{T^m}\colon RU(U(m))\longrightarrow RU(T^m)$,
  which is injective. So we can conclude that
  $(\eta_*(b_m))^\flat_*\allowbreak(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}(\lambda))=1$, as claimed.
  In particular, the class $\eta_*(b_m)$ is invertible.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- rk-6: body_md -->
\label{rk:fix_of_KU}
  As already mentioned, a special feature of the global $K$-theory spectrum ${\mathbf{KU}}$
  is that its geometric fixed points vanish
  for all non-cyclic compact Lie groups.
  The classical folklore proof proceeds via the Euler classes of unitary representations,
  but I do not know a reference. Here is an independent proof that
  uses our results on the pre-Bott classes.

  We let $G$ be a non-cyclic compact Lie group. 
  Theorem \ref{thm:rep_with_trivial_Phi-Lie} provides a unitary $G$-representation $V$
  with $V^G=0$ such that $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$ in $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.  
  Because $\eta\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ inverts all pre-Bott classes $b_m$
  by Theorem \ref{thm:pre-Bott},
  and because $b_{G,V}$ is a restriction of some $b_m$ along a continuous homomorphism,
  $\eta$ also inverts the class  $b_{G,V}$ by Proposition \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert}.
  Hence the class $\Phi^G(\eta_*(b_{G,V}))=\Phi_*^G(\eta)(\Phi^G(b_{G,V})) $ is simultaneously
  invertible and zero. So the ring $\Phi^G_0({\mathbf{KU}})$ is trivial.
<!-- end rk-6 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:geomfix}
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$
  be a morphism of commutative global ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})=RU(T)$.
  Then for every compact Lie group $G$,
  the morphism of geometric fixed point rings
  \[ \Phi^G_*(\eta)\ : \ \Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \longrightarrow \ \Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}}) \]
  is a localization by the set of classes $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})$
  for all unitary $G$-representations $V$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
If the group $G$ is not cyclic,
  then Theorem \ref{thm:rep_with_trivial_Phi-Lie} provides a $G$-representation $V$ with $V^G=0$
  such that $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})=0$
  in the ring $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
  So the localization of $\Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ by $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})$ is trivial.
  Since $\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})$ is also trivial, for example by Remark \ref{rk:fix_of_KU},
  the claim holds for all non-cyclic groups.

  Now we treat the case where $G$ is cyclic, hence abelian.
  Then all irreducible $G$-representations are 1-dimensional,
  so we must show that $\Phi^G_*(\eta)$ is a localization away
  from the classes $\Phi^G(b_{G,\lambda})$ for all continuous homomorphisms $\lambda\colon G\longrightarrow T$.
  The following diagram of graded rings commutes because
  \[ \Phi^G_*(\eta)(\alpha^\sharp)\ = \ \Phi^G_*(\eta)(\Phi^G(\alpha^*(e_T))) \ = \  \Phi^G(\alpha^*(\eta_*(e_T))) \ = \ \Phi^G(\alpha^*[\nu_1])\ ,  \]
  and by naturality and multiplicativity of the geometric fixed point maps:
    \[ \xymatrix@C=30mm{
      {\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)]\otimes \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[d]_{{\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)]\otimes\pi_*(\eta)}
      \ar[rr]_-\cong^-{\alpha\otimes x\mapsto \alpha^\sharp\cdot p_G^*(x)} &&
      \Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[d]^{\Phi^G_*(\eta)}\\
      {\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)]\otimes K U_* \ar[r]_-\cong^-{\alpha\otimes x\mapsto \alpha^*[\nu_1]\cdot p_G^*(x)} \ar@<-1ex>@/_1pc/[rr]_(.2){\alpha\otimes x\mapsto \Phi^G(\alpha^*[\nu_1])\cdot p_G^*(x)}
      & \pi_*^G({\mathbf{KU}}) \ar[r]^-{\Phi^G}    &\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})
    } \]
  The upper horizontal map is an isomorphism by Proposition \ref{prop:monomial_basis} (ii);
  the left lower horizontal map is an isomorphism because $G$ is abelian,
  and hence all irreducible $G$-representations are 1-dimensional.
  We showed in Remark \ref{rk:preBott2Bott} that $\eta$ sends the pre-Bott class $b_1$
  to the $T$-equivariant Bott class $\beta_{T,\nu_1}$.
  So the underlying morphism of non-equivariant ring spectra
  sends the classical non-equivariant pre-Bott class $b_{\operatorname{cl}}=\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(b_1)$
  in $\pi_2(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$  to the classical Bott class in $\pi_2({\mathbf{KU}})$.
  By Snaith's theorem, the morphism
  $\eta_*\colon \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})\longrightarrow K U_*$ of non-equivariant
  homotopy rings is a localization by $b_{\operatorname{cl}}$.
  So the left vertical morphism in the diagram is a localization by $1\otimes b_{\operatorname{cl}}$.

  If $\lambda\colon G\longrightarrow T$ is nontrivial, then
  $\Phi^G(b_{G,\lambda})=1-\lambda^\sharp$ by \eqref{eq:Phi^G_of_char};
  hence the isomorphism of Proposition \ref{prop:monomial_basis} (i)
  identifies $\Phi^G(b_{G,\lambda})$  with $1-\lambda$.  
  The first two maps in the above composite send $1-\lambda$
  to $1-[\lambda]\in\pi_0^G({\mathbf{KU}})$.
  It is a well-known fact that the geometric fixed point map
  $\Phi^G\colon \pi_*^G({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow \Phi_*^G({\mathbf{KU}})$ is localization away
  from the set of classes $1-[\lambda]$ for all nontrivial
  continuous homomorphisms $\lambda\colon G\longrightarrow T$; we recall the classical argument.
  The global $K$-theory spectrum is $G$-equivariantly complex oriented, with the
  Bott classes as Thom classes.
  So the geometric fixed point morphism $\Phi^G\colon \pi_*^G({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow \Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})$
  presents the target as the localization of the source by
  the Euler classes of all nontrivial irreducible complex $G$-representations,
  see \cite[Proposition 7.4.1]{tomDieck:and representation theory} or
  \cite[Proposition 3.20]{greenlees-may:equivariant_stable}.
  Moreover, the Euler class of $\lambda$ is precisely
  \[ i^*(\beta_{G,\lambda}) \ = \  i^*(\lambda^*(\beta_{T,\nu_1})) \ = \
    \lambda^*(i^*(\beta_{T,\nu_1})) \ = \     \lambda^*(1-[\nu_1]) \ = \ 1-[\lambda]\ . \]
  After inverting the upper horizontal isomorphism in the diagram,
  we have factored the morphism
  $\Phi^G_*(\eta)\colon\allowbreak \Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})$
  as the composite of two localizations:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item a morphism
    $\Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\pi_*^G({\mathbf{KU}})$ that inverts the class
    $p_G^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}})=\Phi^G(b_{G,{\mathbb C}})$ in $\Phi^G_2(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
    arising from the trivial  homomorphism $G\longrightarrow T$;
  \item
    followed by the morphism $\Phi^G\colon \pi_*^G({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow\Phi_*^G({\mathbf{KU}})$
    that inverts the images of the classes $\Phi^G(b_{G,\lambda})$
    for all nontrivial homomorphisms $\lambda\colon G\longrightarrow T$.
  \end{itemize}
  So the composite $\Phi^G_*(\eta)\colon \Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}}) $
  is a localization by the classes
  $\Phi^G(b_{G,\lambda})$ for all continuous homomorphisms $\lambda\colon G\longrightarrow T$, trivial or not.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}\
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item 
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ be a morphism of commutative global ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})$.
  Then $\eta$ is a global localization in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$
  by the pre-Bott classes $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 1}$.
\item
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ be a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})$.
  Then $\eta$ is  an ultra-commutative localization in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$
  by the pre-Bott classes $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 1}$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Theorem \ref{thm:geomfix} witnesses the geometric fixed point criterion
  of Theorem \ref{thm:fix_criterion} for the pre-Bott classes $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 1}$,
  and for the morphism $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$, proving (i).
  In the situation of (ii), the underlying morphism of commutative global ring spectra
  is a global localization in  $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$ by $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 1}$, by (i).
  Theorem \ref{thm:UR2CR} (iii) then shows that $\eta$ is also
  an ultra-commutative localization in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$ by $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 1}$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- defn-6: body_md -->
Let ${\mathcal X}$ be a set of representation-graded $G$-equivariant homotopy classes of
  a commutative $G$-ring spectrum $R$.
  A {\em localization by ${\mathcal X}$}
  is an initial object of the full subcategory of the
  slice category $R\backslash\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$ spanned by the
  ${\mathcal X}$-inverting  morphisms.
<!-- end defn-6 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-G-structured}
  Let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ be a morphism of commutative global ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})=RU(T)$.
  Then the morphism $\eta_G\colon\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}_G$ 
  of commutative $G$-ring spectra is a localization in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$
  by the pre-Bott classes $b_{G,V}$ for all unitary $G$-representations $V$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
We apply the localization recognition of Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg}
  to the presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category ${\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G$
  of $G$-spectra, to the morphism $\eta_G\colon\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}_G$,
  and to the family of geometric fixed point functors
  $\Phi^H\circ\operatorname{res}^G_H\colon{\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p^\wedge$,
  for $H$ ranging over all closed subgroups of $G$.
  These functors are strong symmetric monoidal left adjoints, and jointly conservative.
  The full subcategory ${\mathcal W}$ of $(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)\backslash\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G)$
  is spanned by the morphisms that invert the pre-Bott classes $b_{G,V}$
  for all unitary $G$-representations $V$; it is closed under postcomposition
  by Proposition \ref{prop:invert_inherit} (i),
  and it contains $\eta_G$ by Theorem \ref{thm:pre-Bott}
  and Proposition \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert}.
 
  We claim that hypothesis (c) of Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg} holds for every
  closed subgroup $H$ of $G$.
  Since ${\mathbf{KU}}$ is a global ring spectrum, $\operatorname{res}^G_H({\mathbf{KU}}_G)$ is equivalent to ${\mathbf{KU}}_H$.
  By Theorem \ref{thm:geomfix},
  the morphism $\Phi^H_*(\eta_G)\colon \Phi^H_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)\longrightarrow \Phi^H_*({\mathbf{KU}}_G)$
  is a localization by the set of classes
  $\Phi^H(b_{H,W})$ for all unitary $H$-representations $W$.
  While not every $H$-representation underlies a $G$-representation,
  every $H$-representation is a direct summand in a $G$-representation.
  Since the pre-Bott classes are multiplicative (Theorem \ref{thm:fix of pre-Bott} (ii)),
  and a product in a graded-commutative ring is invertible
  if and only if its factors are, we deduce that
  $\Phi^H_*(\eta_G)$ is also a localization by the set of classes
  $\Phi^H(b_{G,V})$ for all unitary  $G$-representations $V$.

  Any $f\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow P$ in ${\mathcal W}$
  inverts $b_{G,V}$ for all unitary $G$-representations $V$,
  and hence it inverts all the classes $\Phi^H(b_{G,V})$ by
  Propositions \ref{prop:invert_criterion} and \ref{prop:invert_inherit} (ii).
  Since  $\Phi^H_*(\eta_G)\colon\allowbreak\Phi^H_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)\longrightarrow \Phi^H_*({\mathbf{KU}}_G)$
  is a localization by these classes, the morphism $\Phi^H_*(f)$ factors through $\Phi^H_*(\eta_G)$.
  So Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg} applies and shows that $\eta_G\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}_G$
  is a localization by $\{b_{G,V}\}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G)$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- rk-7: body_md -->
Besides commutative $G$-ring spectra, there are even more highly
  structured kinds of genuine equivariant ring spectra:
  the {\em $\infty$-category of ultra-commutative $G$-ring spectra}  $\operatorname{URing}_G$
  is the localization of the 1-category of commutative orthogonal $G$-ring spectra
  at the class of those morphisms that are ${\underline \pi}_*$-isomorphisms
  of underlying orthogonal $G$-spectra.
  A {\em localization} of an ultra-commutative $G$-ring spectrum $R$
  by a set of representation-graded $G$-equivariant homotopy classes
  ${\mathcal X}$ is then an initial object of the full subcategory of the
  slice category $R\backslash\operatorname{URing}_G$ spanned by the ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms.

  Much like in the global context in \eqref{eq:ucom2CR_gl}, one can define a `forgetful' functor
  \[ u_G\ :\ \operatorname{URing}_G\ \longrightarrow\  \operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)  \]
  from the $\infty$-category of ultra-commutative $G$-ring spectra to the
  $\infty$-category of commutative $G$-ring spectra.
  Also like in the global context,
  this forgetful functor is {\em not} an equivalence
  (except when the group $G$ is trivial),
  and one can show that it exhibits the $\infty$-category of ultra-commutative $G$-ring spectra
  as bimonadic over the $\infty$-category of commutative $G$-ring spectra.
   In the $G$-equivariant context, the analogous warning as in the global context applies:
  for ultra-commutative $G$-ring spectra,
  the two localizations in $\operatorname{URing}_G$ and in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$ need not coincide
  in general.

  One can adapt the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:UR2CR} (iii)
  from the global to the $G$-equivariant context to show the following:
  Let $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ be a morphism of ultra-commutative $G$-ring spectra
  such that the underlying morphism $u_G i\colon u_G R\longrightarrow u_G S$
  is a localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$.
  Then $i$ is a localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{URing}_G$.
  In fact, the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:UR2CR} (iii) literally goes through
  in the $G$-equivariant context
  if one uses that the forgetful functor $u_G$ is bimonadic.
  This fact, in turn, can be proved in much the same way as its global analog in
  Theorem \ref{thm:UR_monadic} (iii).
  However, as this paper is already quite long, we will not go
  into a detailed proof.  

  Assuming all this, we obtain the $G$-ultra-commutative analog of
  Theorem \ref{thm:main-G-structured}:
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ be a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})=RU(T)$.
  Then the morphism of ultra-commutative $G$-ring spectra
  $\eta_G\colon\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}_G$ is a localization in $\operatorname{URing}_G$ 
  by the pre-Bott classes $b_{G,V}$ for all unitary $G$-representations $V$.
<!-- end rk-7 -->
<!-- construction-9: body_md -->
Lewis and Mandell \cite[Theorem A.1]{lewis-mandell}
  and Dugger \cite{dugger:multigrade} show that one can make consistent choices of
  invertible $G$-spectra for virtual representations, in the following sense.
  We view the representation ring $RO(G)$ as a
  discrete symmetric monoidal category, i.e., with only identity morphisms,
  and with monoidal product the addition in $RO(G)$.
  This symmetric monoidal structure is extremely strict, in that all coherence isomorphisms,
  for unitality, associativity, and even commutativity, are identities.
  The construction of \cite{dugger:multigrade, lewis-mandell} provides a strong monoidal functor
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:duggerlewismandell}
  {\mathbb S}^\bullet_G\  : \  RO(G)\ \longrightarrow\ h({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)   
  \end{equation}
  with values in smash-invertible objects. Moreover, for every orthogonal $G$-representation $V$,
  the invertible object ${\mathbb S}^{[V]}_G={\mathbb S}^\bullet_G([V])$ is isomorphic in 
  $h({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$ to the suspension spectrum $\Sigma^\infty S^V$,
  but not in any preferred or specified way.   
  The construction proceeds from enumerated choices of representatives for the isomorphism
  classes of irreducible orthogonal $G$-representations $\lambda$,
  plus choices of inverses of $\Sigma^\infty S^\lambda$, including the data
  witnessing the inverse property.
  There is no intrinsic way to make `canonical' choices of these data,
  and the choices affect the resulting $RO(G)$-graded rings.
  For definiteness, we shall work with Dugger's construction,
  because it also enjoys a specific symmetry feature discussed below.
  Other than that, we do not need to know the precise construction
  of \eqref{eq:duggerlewismandell}.
   
  Part of the data of the strong monoidal functor \eqref{eq:duggerlewismandell}
  are isomorphisms
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_omega}
    \omega_{\alpha,\beta}\ : \ {\mathbb S}^{\alpha+\beta}_G\ \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\ {\mathbb S}^\alpha_G \wedge {\mathbb S}^\beta_G
  \end{equation}
  for all $\alpha,\beta\in RO(G)$, which satisfy the associativity constraints.
  We emphasize that the functor ${\mathbb S}^\bullet_G$ is not {\em symmetric} monoidal;
  this is already visible for $G=\{1\}$, where $RO(\{1\})={\mathbb Z}$,
  simply because the twist isomorphism of $S^1\wedge S^1$ has degree $-1$. 
  But the functor ${\mathbb S}_G^\bullet$ has a particular kind of symmetry behavior:
  since ${\mathbb S}_G^{\alpha+\beta}={\mathbb S}_G^{\beta+\alpha}$ is invertible,
  there is a unique invertible element $t_{\alpha,\beta}\in \pi_0^G({\mathbb S})$
  that measures the deviation from symmetry, in the sense that
  the following diagram commutes:
  \[   \xymatrix@C=18mm@R=6mm{
      {\mathbb S}_G^{\alpha+\beta}\ar[r]^-{t_{\alpha,\beta}\cdot -}  \ar[d]_{\omega_{\alpha,\beta}}  &
      {\mathbb S}_G^{\beta+\alpha}\ar[d]^{\omega_{\beta,\alpha}}\\
      {\mathbb S}_G^\alpha\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^\beta \ar[r]_-{\text{symmetry}}  &
      {\mathbb S}_G^\beta\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^\alpha  } \]
  Then clearly $t_{\alpha,\beta}=t_{\beta,\alpha}^{-1}$,
  and $t_{\alpha,0}=1$ by the unitality condition.
  The hexagon coherence conditions between the
  associativity and symmetry isomorphisms in $h({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$,
  and the fact that the isomorphisms $\omega_{\alpha,\beta}$ are associative yield
  the relations
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:t_biadd}
    t_{\alpha,\gamma}\cdot t_{\beta,\gamma}\ = \ t_{\alpha+\beta,\gamma}   \text{\quad and \quad}
    t_{\alpha,\beta}\cdot t_{\alpha,\gamma}\ = \ t_{\alpha,\beta+\gamma}
  \end{equation}
  for all $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ in $RO(G)$.
  Moreover, the element $\varepsilon_\alpha=t_{\alpha,\alpha}$ in $\pi_0^G({\mathbb S})$ 
  satisfies $\varepsilon_\alpha^2=1$, and it equals the trace of the identity of ${\mathbb S}^\alpha_G$,
  and hence the Euler characteristic of the invertible object ${\mathbb S}^\alpha_G$.
  The relations \eqref{eq:t_biadd}
  imply that the units $t_{\alpha,\beta}$ are determined by the special cases
  where $\alpha=[\lambda]$ and $\beta=[\mu]$ are the classes of two irreducible
  representations $\lambda$ and $\mu$. A property of Dugger's construction is
  that $t_{[\lambda],[\mu]}=1$ whenever $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are non-isomorphic irreducibles.
  So in fact
  \[ t_{\alpha,\beta}\ = \ \prod_{\lambda} \varepsilon_{[\lambda]}^{m(\lambda,\alpha)\cdot m(\lambda,\beta)}\ ,\]
  where the product is over a set of representatives of the isomorphism
  classes of irreducible representations, and $m(\lambda,\alpha)\in{\mathbb Z}$
  is the multiplicity of $\lambda$ in $\alpha$, compare \cite[Proposition 1.2]{dugger:multigrade}.
  
  For later use in Construction \ref{con:RO(G) pre-Bott} we note that
  $\varepsilon_{[\lambda]}=1$ whenever the orthogonal representation $\lambda$
  underlies a unitary $G$-representation, simply because for every
  unitary $G$-representation $W$, the twist self-isometry of $S^{W\oplus W}$
  is equivariantly homotopic to the identity.
  Moreover, if $\lambda$ is an irreducible orthogonal representation of real type,
  then it occurs in any unitary representation with even multiplicity.
  Consequently, the symmetry markers $t_{\alpha,\beta}$ equal $1$
  whenever $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are in the image of the forgetful homomorphism $RU(G)\longrightarrow RO(G)$.
<!-- end construction-9 -->
<!-- construction-10: body_md -->
\label{con:pi_star^G}
  The strong monoidal functor ${\mathbb S}^\bullet_G$ from \eqref{eq:duggerlewismandell}
  allows us to introduce $RO(G)$-graded $G$-equivariant homotopy groups,
  as follows. For a $G$-spectrum $X$ and a virtual representation $\alpha\in RO(G)$,
  we set
  \[ \pi_\alpha^G(X)\ = \ h({\mathcal S} p_G)({\mathbb S}_G^\alpha,X)\ ,\]
  the abelian group of morphisms, in the homotopy category of $G$-spectra,
  from ${\mathbb S}_G^\alpha$ to $X$.
  Since the object  ${\mathbb S}_G^\alpha$ is invertible, it is in particular compact
  in $h({\mathcal S} p_G)$, so the functor $\pi_\alpha^G$ sends arbitrary coproducts
  to direct sums.  We shall write
  \[ \pi_\star^G(X)\ = \ \{\pi_\alpha^G(X)\}_{\alpha\in RO(G)} \]
  for the resulting $RO(G)$-graded abelian group.

  If $Y$ is another $G$-spectrum and $\beta\in RO(G)$, we obtain a biadditive pairing
  \begin{align}\label{eq:RO-sm}
  \wedge \ : \   \pi_\alpha^G(X)\times \pi_\beta^G(Y)\quad
    = \quad  &h({\mathcal S} p_G)({\mathbb S}_G^\alpha,X)\times h({\mathcal S} p_G)({\mathbb S}_G^\beta,Y)\\
        \xrightarrow{\quad \wedge \quad}\  &h({\mathcal S} p_G)({\mathbb S}_G^\alpha\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^\beta,X\wedge Y)\nonumber\\
    \xrightarrow[\eqref{eq:define_omega}]{-\circ \omega_{\alpha,\beta}}\  &h({\mathcal S} p_G)({\mathbb S}_G^{\alpha+\beta},X\wedge Y)\ =\ \pi_{\alpha+\beta}^G(X\wedge Y)\ .\nonumber
  \end{align}
   It is a routine check, using that the functor ${\mathbb S}_G^\bullet$ is monoidal,
   that these pairings are associative and unital.
   Since the functor ${\mathbb S}_G^\bullet$ is not symmetric monoidal,
   the pairing is not strictly commutative, which is already the case for
   the usual ${\mathbb Z}$-grading in stable homotopy theory.
   The deviation from strict commutativity is measured by the units $t_{\alpha,\beta}$,
   in the sense that
   \[ x\wedge y \ =\ t_{\alpha,\beta}\cdot (\tau_{Y,X})_*(y\wedge x)
     \text{\quad   in $\pi_{\alpha+\beta}^G(X\wedge Y)$,} \]
   for all $x\in \pi_\alpha^G(X)$ and $y\in\pi_\beta^G(Y)$.
   Here $\tau_{Y,X}\colon Y\wedge X\longrightarrow X\wedge Y$ denotes the symmetry equivalence for
   the smash product of $G$-spectra.
   
   Now we let $R$ be a homotopy $G$-ring spectrum
   with multiplication morphism $\mu\colon R\wedge R\longrightarrow R$ in $h({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$.
   Then the composite maps
   \begin{equation}\label{eq:RO_product}
 \cdot \ : \ \pi_\alpha^G(R)\times \pi_\beta^G(R)\ \xrightarrow{\ \wedge \ }\
    \pi_{\alpha+\beta}^G(R\wedge R)\ \xrightarrow{\ \mu_*\ }\
    \pi_{\alpha+\beta}^G(R)       
   \end{equation}
  enhance $\pi_\star^G(R)$ to an $RO(G)$-graded ring.
  And for every left homotopy $R$-module $M$
  in $h({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$, the composite maps
  \[ \pi_\alpha^G(R)\times \pi_\beta^G(M)\ \xrightarrow{\ \wedge \ }\
    \pi_{\alpha+\beta}^G(R\wedge M)\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{act}_*\ }\
    \pi_{\alpha+\beta}^G(M)   \]
  enhance $\pi_\star^G(M)$ to an $RO(G)$-graded left $\pi_\star^G(R)$-module.
  If the multiplication of $R$ is homotopy-commutative,
  then
  $\pi_\star^G(R)$ is a `graded-commutative' $RO(G)$-graded ring,
  in the sense that
  \[ y\cdot x \ =\ t_{\alpha,\beta}\cdot (x\cdot y)
     \text{\quad   in $\pi_{\beta+\alpha}^G(R)$,} \]
   for all $x\in \pi_\alpha^G(R)$ and $y\in\pi_\beta^G(R)$.
<!-- end construction-10 -->
<!-- construction-11: body_md -->
\label{con:RO(G) pre-Bott}
  We let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  As we shall now explain, we can make `consistent' choices
  of pre-Bott classes $\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V\rangle}\in \pi_{[V]}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)$
  in the $RO(G)$-graded homotopy ring.
  These are indexed by effective classes in $RU(G)$,
  i.e., ones represented by actual unitary $G$-representations;
  as the notation suggests, the class $\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V\rangle}$ only depends
  on the isomorphism class $\langle V\rangle$ of $V$ in $RU(G)$,
  but not on the specific representative.
  One should mind the appearance of both $RU(G)$ and $RO(G)$:
  the classes $\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V\rangle}$ are defined for effective elements
  in the complex representation ring $RU(G)$, but they live in the
  $RO(G)$-graded homotopy ring, in the degree of the underlying
  orthogonal $G$-representation.
  
  For the construction, we choose representatives $\{\mu_i\}_{i\in I}$
  for the isomorphism classes of irreducible unitary $G$-representations.
  For every chosen representative, we choose an equivalence of $G$-spectra
  $\kappa_i\colon {\mathbb S}_G^{[\mu_i]}\cong\Sigma^\infty S^{\mu_i}$,
  where $[\mu_i]$ is the class in $RO(G)$ of the underlying orthogonal
  $G$-representation of $\mu_i$. Then we define
  \[ \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle \mu_i\rangle}\ = \
    \kappa^*_i(b_{G,\mu_i})\ \in \ \pi_{[\mu_i]}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)\ .\]
  A general unitary $G$-representation $V$ is isomorphic to
  $\mu_{i_1}\oplus\dots\oplus\mu_{i_k}$
  for suitable $i_1,\dots,i_k\in I$, and we set
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:RO-pre-Bott}
    \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V\rangle}\ = \
    \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle \mu_{i_1}\rangle}\cdot\ldots\cdot \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle \mu_{i_k}\rangle}
    \ \in \ \pi_{[V]}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)  \ ,  
  \end{equation}
  where the product is taken in the $RO(G)$-graded homotopy ring as in \eqref{eq:RO_product}.
  As mentioned above, the symmetry markers $t_{\alpha,\beta}$ equal $1$
  whenever $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are in the image of the forgetful homomorphism $RU(G)\longrightarrow RO(G)$.
  Hence the class \eqref{eq:RO-pre-Bott} does not depend on the ordering of the
  irreducible summands of $V$, and moreover
  \[ \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V\rangle}\cdot \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle W\rangle}\ = \ \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V\oplus W\rangle}\ .\]
  A final property is the following consistency: for every unitary $G$-representation $V$,
  there is an equivalence $\kappa_V\colon {\mathbb S}_G^{[V]}\xrightarrow{\sim}\Sigma^\infty S^V$
  such that $\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V\rangle}=\kappa_V^*(b_{G,V})$.
  Indeed, we may choose a ${\mathbb C}$-linear $G$-equivariant isometry
  $\psi\colon\mu_{i_1}\oplus\dots\oplus\mu_{i_k}\cong V$, and then the composite equivalence
  \begin{align*}
    {\mathbb S}_G^{[V]}\ = \ {\mathbb S}_G^{[\mu_{i_1}]+\dots+[\mu_{i_k}]} \ \xrightarrow{\omega_{[\mu_{i_1}],\dots,[\mu_{i_k}]}}\
    &{\mathbb S}_G^{[\mu_{i_1}]}\wedge \dots\wedge{\mathbb S}_G^{[\mu_{i_k}]} \\
    \xrightarrow{\kappa_{i_1}\wedge\dots\wedge\kappa_{i_k}}\ &(\Sigma^\infty S^{\mu_{i_1}})\wedge\dots\wedge(\Sigma^\infty S^{\mu_{i_k}})\\
    \cong \quad &\Sigma^\infty S^{\mu_{i_1}\oplus\dots\oplus\mu_{i_k}}\ \xrightarrow{\ \Sigma^\infty S^\psi\ } \
                 \Sigma^\infty S^V
  \end{align*}
  has the desired property.
<!-- end construction-11 -->
<!-- construction-12: body_md -->
We choose an exhaustive sequence
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:exhaust}
    U_1 \ , \ U_2 \ , \ U_3\  , \ \dots    
  \end{equation}
  of finite-dimensional unitary $G$-representations,
  i.e., such that every finite-dimensional unitary $G$-re\-presen\-ta\-tion
  embeds, equivariantly and ${\mathbb C}$-linearly, into 
  \[ V_n\ =  \ U_1\oplus\dots\oplus U_n\]
  for sufficiently large $n$.
  We set
  \[ \alpha_n\ =  \ [V_n]\ = \ [U_1\oplus\dots\oplus U_n] \]
  in $RO(G)$, including $\alpha_0=0$.
  We represent the pre-Bott class $\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle U_n\rangle}\in\pi_{[U_n]}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)$
  by a morphism
  \[ h_n\ : \ \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_{n-1}}\ \longrightarrow \
    \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G \wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n} \]
  in $\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$, i.e.,
  such that 
  \[ h_n(1\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_{n-1}})\ =\ \mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle U_n\rangle}\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n} \ ,\]
  where the pairing on the right hand side is
  the $RO(G)$-graded external multiplication  
  \[ \wedge \ : \ \pi_{[U_n]}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)\times \pi^G_{-\alpha_n}({\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n})\
    \longrightarrow \
    \pi_{-\alpha_{n-1}}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G\wedge{\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n})  \]
  defined in \eqref{eq:RO-sm}; this defines the morphism $h_n$ uniquely up to homotopy.
  The sequence of morphisms
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:KU_G-sequence}
    \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\xrightarrow{\ h_1\ } 
    \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\wedge {\mathbb S}^{-\alpha_1}_G \xrightarrow{\ h_2\ }
    \dots \xrightarrow{\ h_n\ } \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n} \dots
  \end{equation}
  then determines a functor
  $F\colon {\mathbb N}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$.

 We let $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G$ act on ${\mathbf{KU}}_G$ through the morphism
 $\eta_G$ of commutative $G$-ring spectra, making ${\mathbf{KU}}_G$ an object of
 $\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$. We define 
 \[ k_n\ :\  \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\wedge {\mathbb S}^{-\alpha_n}_G \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathbf{KU}}_G \]
 as a morphism in $\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$,
 again unique up to homotopy, such that
 \[  k_n(1\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n})\ =\ (\eta_*(\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V_n\rangle}))^{-1} \ , \]
 where we exploit that the morphism $\eta_G$ inverts all pre-Bott classes.
 The relations
  \[ \eta_*(\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle U_n\rangle})\cdot  (\eta_*(\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V_n\rangle}))^{-1} =
    \eta_*(\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle U_n\rangle})\cdot  (  \eta_*(\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle U_n\rangle})
   \cdot\eta_*(\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V_{n-1}\rangle}) )^{-1} = (\eta_*(\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle V_{n-1}\rangle}))^{-1} \]
  in $\pi_{-\alpha_{n-1}}^G({\mathbf{KU}}_G)$ show that
  $k_n\circ h_n$ equals $k_{n-1}$ in the homotopy category
  $h(\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge))$.
  We choose homotopies witnessing this, and they 
  extend the functor  $F\colon {\mathbb N}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$ to a cocone diagram
  $\bar F\colon {\mathbb N}^\triangleright\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$.
<!-- end construction-12 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:telescopic localization}
  Let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ be a morphism of commutative global ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})=RU(T)$.
  Then the cocone diagram  $\bar F\colon {\mathbb N}^\triangleright\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$
  presents ${\mathbf{KU}}_G$ as a colimit in $\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$
  of the sequence \eqref{eq:KU_G-sequence}.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The forgetful functor $u\colon\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p_G$
  preserves colimits and is conservative.
  The geometric fixed point functors $\Phi^H\circ\operatorname{res}^G_H\colon {\mathcal S} p_G\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p$
  preserve colimits, and are jointly conservative for all closed subgroups of $G$.
  And the functor $\pi_*\colon {\mathcal S} p\longrightarrow \operatorname{GrAb}$ is conservative and preserves sequential colimits.
  So it suffices to show that
  $\pi_*\circ \Phi^H\circ\operatorname{res}^G_H\circ u\circ\bar F\colon {\mathbb N}^\triangleright\longrightarrow\operatorname{GrAb}$ is a colimit,
  for all $H\leq G$.
  Since the $\{U_i\}$ are an exhaustive sequence of $G$-representations,
  the underlying $H$-representations are also exhaustive,
  and thus contain every irreducible $H$-representation infinitely often.
  So the colimit of $\pi_*\circ \Phi^H\circ\operatorname{res}^G_H\circ u\circ F\colon {\mathbb N}\longrightarrow\operatorname{GrAb}$
  calculates the localization of the geometric fixed point ring $\Phi^H_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)$
  obtained by inverting the classes  $\Phi^H(b_{H,\lambda})$ for all irreducible
  $H$-representations $\lambda$. 
  By Theorem \ref{thm:geomfix}, the morphism $\Phi^H_*(\eta_G)$ exhibits $\Phi^H_*({\mathbf{KU}}_G)$
  as such a localization.
  Hence $\pi_*\circ \Phi^H\circ\operatorname{res}^G_H\circ u\circ \bar F$ is a colimit
  for all $H\leq G$, and so
  $\bar F\colon {\mathbb N}^\triangleright\longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)$
  is a colimit, too.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-G-RO-version}
  Let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  Let $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}$ be a morphism of commutative global ring spectra
  such that $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})=RU(T)$.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item For every $\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G$-module $M$ in ${\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge$,
    the morphism
    \[ \pi_\star^G(\eta_G\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G} M)\ : \  \pi_\star^G(M)  \ \longrightarrow \ \pi_\star^G({\mathbf{KU}}_G\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G} M) \]
    exhibits the target as a localization,
    in $RO(G)$-graded  $\pi_\star^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G)$-modules,
    of the source by the set of pre-Bott classes of all unitary $G$-representations.
   \item For every finite based $G$-CW-complex $A$, the morphism 
    \[  \eta^\star_G(A)\ : \  (\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G)^\star(A)  \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathbf{KU}}_G^\star(A) \]
    exhibits the target as a localization,
    in $RO(G)$-graded  $(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G)^\star$-modules,
    of the source by the set of pre-Bott classes of all unitary $G$-representations.
  \item The morphism of graded-commutative $RO(G)$-graded rings
    \[  \pi_\star^G(\eta_G)\ : \  \pi_\star^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G) \ \longrightarrow \ \pi_\star^G({\mathbf{KU}}_G) \]
    exhibits the target as an $RO(G)$-graded localization of the source by the set
    of pre-Bott classes of all unitary $G$-representations.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
(i)  The functor
  $-\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}M\colon\operatorname{Mod}_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}({\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge)\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p_G$
  preserves all colimits. 
  So Theorem \ref{thm:telescopic localization}
  shows that the cocone diagram
  $\bar F\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}M\colon {\mathbb N}^\triangleright\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p_G$
  presents ${\mathbf{KU}}_G\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}M$
  as a colimit in ${\mathcal S} p_G$ of the sequence
\[ 
    M\xrightarrow{M\wedge h_1}  M\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_1} \xrightarrow{M\wedge h_2}
    \dots \xrightarrow{M\wedge h_n}  M\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n} \dots\ .
 \]
  We have exploited
  \[  (\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n})\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}M
    \ \cong \ M\wedge {\mathbb S}_G^{-\alpha_n}\ . \]
  By design, the morphism $M\wedge h_n$ induces multiplication
  by the pre-Bott class $\mathbbm{b}_{G,\langle U_n\rangle}$ on $RO(G)$-graded homotopy groups.

  For every $\alpha\in RO(G)$, the functor $\pi_\alpha^G\colon {\mathcal S} p_G\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ab}$
  preserves sequential colimits. 
  So $\pi_\star^G({\mathbf{KU}}_G\allowbreak\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}M)$ is exhibited
  as a sequential colimit, over multiplications by pre-Bott classes,
  of appropriate $RO(G)$-graded shifts of instances of $\pi_\star^G(M)$.
  Since the sequence of $G$-representations \eqref{eq:exhaust} is exhaustive,
  the algebraic effect of the sequential colimit
  is precisely $RO(G)$-graded localization by the pre-Bott classes
  of all unitary $G$-representations.

  (ii) By the finiteness of $A$, the assembly morphism
  \[ \operatorname{map}_*(A,\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G}{\mathbf{KU}}_G \ \longrightarrow \
    \operatorname{map}_*(A,{\mathbf{KU}}_G) \]
  is an equivalence of ${\mathbf{KU}}_G$-modules. So part (ii) follows from part (i),
  applied to the $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G$-module $\operatorname{map}_*(A,\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G)$.

  (iii) The localization property in the category of graded-commutative $RO(G)$-graded rings
  is detected by the analogous localization property of the underlying
  $RO(G)$-graded  $\pi_\star^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G)$-modules.
  So property (iii) follows from (i) for $M=\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- rk-8: body_md -->
The effect of the morphism $\eta_G\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}_G$
  on equivariant cohomology theories has previously received some attention
  under the heading `Segal--Becker splitting'.
  Segal \cite{segal:CP infty} and Becker \cite{becker:characteristic_and_K}
  showed in the non-equivariant context that the transformation of
  cohomology theories induced by $\eta$ is split surjective; in fact,
  the induced map of infinite loop spaces
  $\Omega^\infty\eta\colon \Omega^\infty(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbb C} P^\infty)\longrightarrow \Omega^\infty K U\sim {\mathbb Z}\times BU$
  admits a section by a loop map.
  The Segal--Becker splitting was generalized to the equivariant context by
  Iriye and Kono  \cite{iriye-kono:Segal-Becker KG} for finite groups,
  and by Crabb \cite{crabb:brauer} for general compact Lie groups.
  It says that for every finite $G$-CW-complex $A$, the map
