  \begin{equation}\label{eq:split_epi}
    \eta_G^0(A)\ :\ (\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})^0_G(A)\ \longrightarrow\ {\mathbf{KU}}_G^0(A)
  \end{equation}
  is a naturally split epimorphism.
  Since the map \eqref{eq:split_epi} is surjective already before any localization,
  its extension to the algebraic $RO(G)$-graded localization
  by the pre-Bott classes is also surjective.
  Hence the new insight provided by Theorem \ref{thm:main-G-RO-version} (ii) is the fact that
  every element in the kernel of \eqref{eq:split_epi} is `pre-Bott torsion',
  i.e., annihilated by the pre-Bott class of some unitary $G$-representation.
<!-- end rk-8 -->
<!-- prop-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:modulo_torsion}
  Let $C$ be a cyclic group of prime order $p$.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item 
    The composite
    \[ \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})[b_{\operatorname{nv}}]\ \longrightarrow \
      \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \xrightarrow{\text{\em proj}} \
      \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})/\text{\em (torsion)}  \]
    is an isomorphism of graded rings.
  \item The morphism $\pi_*^C(\eta)\colon\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\pi_*^C({\mathbf{KU}})$
    is not a localization of graded-commutative rings by any subset
    of homogeneous elements of the source.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
(i) The abelian group $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ is torsion-free,
  see for example \cite[Corollary 4.1.13]{schwede:global};
  so the result is tautologically true in dimension zero.
  By design, the graded ring $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})[b_{\operatorname{nv}}]$ is concentrated
  in even degrees, and the class $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$ acts bijectively in non-negative degrees.
  Since the claim holds in dimension 0, it remains to show that 
  the graded ring $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ is torsion in all odd degrees,
  and the naive pre-Bott class acts bijectively modulo torsion, i.e.,
  \[ -\cdot b_{\operatorname{nv}}\ \colon \ \pi_k^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})/\text{(torsion)}
    \ \longrightarrow \ \pi_{k+2}^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})/\text{(torsion)}  \]
  is bijective for all $k\geq 0$.
  
  We use the classical fact that the composite
  \[ {\mathbb Z}[b_{\operatorname{cl}}] \ \longrightarrow \ \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty)\ \xrightarrow{\text{proj}} \
    \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty)/\text{(torsion)}  \]
  is an isomorphism of graded rings, with $b_{\operatorname{cl}}=\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(b_1)$
  the classical pre-Bott class. Indeed, the quotient of
  $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty)$ by its torsion ideal
  embeds into ${\mathbb Q}\otimes\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty)\allowbreak\cong H_*({\mathbb C} P^\infty;{\mathbb Q})={\mathbb Q}[b_{\operatorname{cl}}]$,
  and the powers of $b_{\operatorname{cl}}$ cannot be divisible because their images in $\pi_*(KU)$
  are not divisible.
  In particular,
  $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty)$ is torsion in odd degrees, and
  the classical pre-Bott class acts bijectively modulo torsion.

  For the suspension spectrum of any $C$-space $X$, the geometric fixed point
  homomorphism is a split epimorphism.
  So the isotropy separation sequence becomes a split short exact sequence:
  \[ 0 \longrightarrow \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ (EC \times X)) \xrightarrow{\ q_*\ }
    \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ X) \xrightarrow{\ \Phi^C\ }  \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ X^C) \longrightarrow 0     \]
  Here $q\colon EC\times X\longrightarrow X$ is the projection.
  Since the sequence is split exact, it remains exact after dividing out the torsion subgroups
  everywhere.
  
  Now we specialize to $X={\mathbf P}_C$, the underlying $C$-space of the global space ${\mathbf P}$.
  We let $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$ act on $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ ({\mathbf P}_C)^C)\cong\Phi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$
  by multiplication by the class $\Phi^C(b_{\operatorname{nv}})$.
  The torsion subgroups are invariant under the $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$-action,
  so we arrive at a short exact sequence of graded ${\mathbb Z}[b_{\operatorname{nv}}]$-modules:
  \[      0 \longrightarrow \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ (EC \times {\mathbf P}_C))/(\text{tors.}) \xrightarrow{\ q_*\ }
    \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})/(\text{tors.}) \xrightarrow{\ \Phi^C\ } 
    \Phi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})/(\text{tors.}) \longrightarrow 0 \]
  The above classical fact and the description of
  Proposition \ref{prop:monomial_basis} (ii) show that the term
  $\Phi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})/\allowbreak(\text{torsion})$  is trivial in all odd degrees,
  and that $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$ acts bijectively on it.
  
  We claim that also
  $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ (EC\times {\mathbf P}_C))/(\text{torsion})$ is trivial in odd degrees,
  and $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$ acts bijectively on it.
  Granted this, the five lemma shows that $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$ acts bijectively on
  $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})/(\text{torsion})$, which is also concentrated in even degrees.

  Since ${\mathbf P}$ is a global classifying space for the circle group $T$,
  the $C$-space ${\mathbf P}_C$ is $C$-homotopy equivalent to $(E_C T)/T$,
  with $E_C T$ a universal $(C\times T)$-space for the family of graph subgroups
  of $C\times T$, see \cite[Proposition 1.1.26 (i)]{schwede:global}.
  The $(C\times T)$-space $EC\times (E_C T)$ is free and underlying contractible,
  so
  \[ EC\times_C{\mathbf P}_C\ \simeq \  (EC\times (E_C T))/(C\times T)\ \simeq \
    B(C\times T) \ \simeq\ BC \times {\mathbb C} P^\infty \]
  is a non-equivariant classifying space for $C\times T$.
  The Adams isomorphism thus identifies $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ (EC \times {\mathbf P}_C))$
  with the non-equivariant stable homotopy groups $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ (BC \times {\mathbb C} P^\infty))$.
  A choice of basepoint of $B C$ splits this graded group as the direct sum of
  \[ \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty) \text{\quad and\quad}
    \pi_*((\Sigma^\infty  B C)\wedge {\mathbb C} P^\infty_+)\ .\]
  The second of these summands is $p$-power torsion because the reduced suspension spectrum
  $\Sigma^\infty BC$ becomes trivial in the stable homotopy category after inverting $p$;
  so it contributes a torsion direct summand to $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ (EC \times {\mathbf P}_C))$.
  The torsion subgroup is $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$-invariant, so 
  $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ (EC\times {\mathbf P}_C))/(\text{torsion})$ 
  is ${\mathbb Z}[b_{\operatorname{nv}}]$-linearly isomorphic to
  $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty)/(\text{torsion})$,
  with $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$ acting as the classical pre-Bott class $b_{\operatorname{cl}}$.
  One more time by the above classical fact,
  $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$ indeed acts bijectively on $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb C} P^\infty)/(\text{torsion})$,
  and hence also on $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+ (EC\times {\mathbf P}_C))/(\text{torsion})$, as claimed. 
  This completes the proof of (i).
  
  (ii)   We show first that the ring homomorphism
  $\pi_0^C(\eta)\colon  \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\pi_0^C({\mathbf{KU}})$
  is not a localization by any multiplicative subset of the source.
  We argue by contradiction and suppose that $\pi_0^C(\eta)$ presents $\pi_0^C({\mathbf{KU}})$
  as a localization by a multiplicative subset $S$ of $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
  We set $\xi=\operatorname{res}^T_C(e_T)\in \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$, for some embedding $C\longrightarrow T$.
  The abelian group $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ is free of rank $p+1$,
  with basis the classes $\xi^k$ for $0\leq k\leq p-1$,
  and the class $t=\operatorname{tr}_{\{1\}}^C(1)$, see for example \cite[Corollary 4.1.13]{schwede:global}.
  The ring structure is determined by the relations
  \[ \xi^p \ = \ 1\ ,\quad   \xi\cdot t\  = \ t  \text{\quad and\quad} t^2 \ = \ p\cdot t\  . \]  
  The kernel of $\pi_0^C(\eta)$ is free of rank 1 as an abelian group,  generated by the element 
  \[ \kappa\ =\ (1+\xi+\dots+\xi^{p-1})- t \ . \]
  The localization property provides an element $s\in S$ such that $s\cdot \kappa=0$.
  The ring homomorphism $\pi_0^C(\eta)$
  has a section $\sigma\colon\pi_0^C({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  by a ring homomorphism, determined by sending $\operatorname{res}^T_C[\nu_1]=\pi_0^C(\eta)(\xi)$
  to the element $\xi$ in $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
  The element $\pi_0^C(\eta)(s)$ is a unit in $\pi_0^C({\mathbf{KU}})$ by the localization property.
  So $u=\sigma(\pi_0^C(\eta)(s))$ is a unit in $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$,
  and $\pi_0^C(\eta)(s\cdot u^{-1})=1$.
  Hence
  \[ s \ = \ u\cdot(1+ a\kappa) \]
  for some $a\in{\mathbb Z}$, because $\kappa$ generates the kernel of $\pi_0^C(\eta)$.
  The relation $\kappa^2=p\cdot\kappa$ yields
  \[ s\cdot \kappa \ = \ u\cdot(1+ a\kappa)\cdot \kappa
    \ = \ u\cdot(1+ p a)\cdot \kappa\ .  \]
  Since $\kappa$ is not a torsion element, $(1+pa)\cdot\kappa$ is non-zero,
  and hence $s\cdot\kappa$ is non-zero.
  We have arrived at a contradiction, so $\pi_0^C(\eta)$
  is not a localization by any multiplicative subset, as claimed.

  Now we show that the composite
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:2nd_compo}
    \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})[b_{\operatorname{nv}}]\ \longrightarrow \
    \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \xrightarrow{\pi_*^C(\eta)} \
    \pi_*^C({\mathbf{KU}}) = \pi_0^C({\mathbf{KU}})[\beta_{\operatorname{nv}}^\pm]    
  \end{equation}
  is not a localization of graded-commutative rings by any set of homogeneous elements of
  the source, where $\beta_{\operatorname{nv}}=\pi_2^C(\eta)(b_{\operatorname{nv}})=p_C^*(\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(\beta_{T,\nu_1}))\in \pi_2^C({\mathbf{KU}})$.
  Again we argue by contradiction and suppose that  \eqref{eq:2nd_compo}
  were a localization by such a set ${\mathcal Y}$.
  We write each element of this set as $y=w\cdot b_{\operatorname{nv}}^k$,
  with $w\in \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ and $k\geq 0$.
  Then $k$ must be positive for at least one element of ${\mathcal Y}$,
  for else the localization would be concentrated in non-negative degrees.
  Inverting $y$ can be achieved by first inverting $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$, if $k>0$, and then inverting $w$.
  Hence the extension of \eqref{eq:2nd_compo} to a homomorphism
  \[ \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})[b_{\operatorname{nv}}^\pm]\ \longrightarrow \ \pi_0^C({\mathbf{KU}})[\beta_{\operatorname{nv}}^\pm]\]
  is a localization by the set of factors $w$ of degree 0 in the above products.
  Thus $\pi_0^C(\eta)\colon\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\pi_0^C({\mathbf{KU}})$
  is a localization by the set of these $w$, contradicting the previous paragraph.

  Now we prove part (ii) by contradiction and suppose that
  $\pi_*^C(\eta)\colon \pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\allowbreak\longrightarrow\pi_*^C({\mathbf{KU}})$
  were a localization by a set ${\mathcal Y}$ of homogeneous elements of the source.
  Since $\pi_*^C({\mathbf{KU}})$ is torsion-free, every torsion element of
  $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ lies in the kernel of $\pi_*^C(\eta)$.
  Since localization is exact, any localization of $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ by ${\mathcal Y}$
  is thus also a localization of
  $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})/(\text{torsion})$ by the image of ${\mathcal Y}$.
  Part (i) identifies $\pi_*^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})/(\text{torsion})$
  with $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})[b_{\operatorname{nv}}]$, so we deduce that the composite \eqref{eq:2nd_compo}
  is a localization, contradicting the previous paragraph.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:no_Z_localization}
  Let $G$ be a nontrivial compact Lie group.  
  There is no set ${\mathcal Y}$ of homogeneous elements of
  the integer-graded ring $\pi_*^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  such that the morphism $\eta_G\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}_G$
  extends to an equivalence of $G$-spectra from the telescopic localization
  of $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G$ by ${\mathcal Y}$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Every nontrivial compact Lie group $G$
  has a closed cyclic subgroup $C\leq G$ of prime order.
  If ${\mathbf{KU}}_G$ were a telescopic localization by a set ${\mathcal Y}$
  of homogeneous elements of $\pi_*^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$,
  then the underlying $C$-spectrum ${\mathbf{KU}}_C$ would be
  a telescopic localization of $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_C$ by the set
  $\{\operatorname{res}^G_C(y)\mid y\in{\mathcal Y}\}$.
  Telescopically inverting a set of integer-graded equivariant homotopy
  classes induces the algebraic localization on equivariant homotopy groups,
  so this would contradict Proposition \ref{prop:modulo_torsion} (ii).
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- rk-9: body_md -->
\label{rk:spitz-oest}
  As already mentioned in the introduction, the paper 
  \cite{spitzweck-oestvaer:equivariant}
  by Spitzweck and {\O}stv{\ae}r claims that for abelian compact Lie groups $A$,
  the spectrum ${\mathbf{KU}}_A$ can be obtained from $\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_A$
  by telescopically inverting a single class in the integer-graded
  homotopy group $\pi_2^A(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_A)$.
  Their class is the analog of our naive pre-Bott class from \eqref{eq:naive_pre-Bott},
  i.e., the inflation  $b_{\operatorname{nv}}=p_A^*(\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(b_1))$ of the non-equivariant Bott class.
  However, the main result \cite[Theorem 1.1]{spitzweck-oestvaer:equivariant}
  contradicts Corollary \ref{cor:no_Z_localization}, and is incorrect.

  The argument of \cite{spitzweck-oestvaer:equivariant} breaks down in their Lemma 3.2,
  which in our notation asserts that $b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}(1-\xi_\infty)$
  is an equivariant orientation of $(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_A)[b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}]$,
  for $\xi_\infty\in (\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})^0_A({\mathbf P}_A)$
  the tautological class, represented by the identity of ${\mathbf P}_A$.
  In other words, the claim is that
  for every $A$-character $\alpha\colon A\longrightarrow T$,
  the restriction of $b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}(1-\xi_\infty)$
  along $P({\mathbb C}\oplus\alpha)\longrightarrow {\mathbf P}_A$
  is a generator of the reduced $A$-equivariant $(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_A)[b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}]$-cohomology
  of $P({\mathbb C}\oplus\alpha)$, based at $P({\mathbb C}\oplus 0)$,
  as a graded module over the ${\mathbb Z}$-graded ring
  $(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_A)[b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}]^*_A$.
  This orientation property is not checked in the proof of 
  \cite[Lemma 3.2]{spitzweck-oestvaer:equivariant},
  and it fails for example when $A$ is cyclic of prime order and $\alpha$ is non-trivial.
  Consequently, in the first step of the proof of
  \cite[Theorem 1.1]{spitzweck-oestvaer:equivariant},
  the appeal to the universality of $MU_A$ is unjustified.

  We claim that the restriction of $1-\xi_\infty$ along 
  \[ S^\alpha\ \xrightarrow{\lambda\mapsto[\bar\lambda:1]}\ P({\mathbb C}\oplus\alpha)\ \longrightarrow\ {\mathbf P}_A \]
  equals $b_{A,\alpha}$ in $\pi_\alpha^A(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_A)$.
  Indeed, this relation holds after restricting further along
  the fixed point inclusion $i\colon S^0\longrightarrow S^\alpha$, by \eqref{eq:i^*_of_b}.
  In the special case $A=T$ and $\alpha=\operatorname{Id}_T$, restriction along $i$ is injective,
  so the claim holds for $(T,\operatorname{Id}_T)$. Naturality for
  restriction along continuous homomorphisms then proves the claim for general $(A,\alpha)$.
  Consequently, $b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}(1-\xi_\infty)$ restricts to $b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}\cdot b_{A,\alpha}$ in
  $\pi_{\alpha-2}^A(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_A)[b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}]$.
  So inverting the pre-Bott classes of all unitary representations,
  as opposed to only inverting $b_{\operatorname{nv}}$,
  is what turns the class $b_{\operatorname{nv}}^{-1}(1-\xi_\infty)$ into an equivariant orientation.
<!-- end rk-9 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:all_different}
  Let $i\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow R$ be an ultra-commutative localization in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$
  by the pre-Bott class $b_m$ for some $m\geq 1$.
  Then $i$ does not invert $b_{m+1}$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
It suffices to exhibit any morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra from
  $ \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ that inverts $b_m$  but not $b_{m+1}$.
  We write ${\mathcal F}_m$ for the global class of compact Lie groups
  that are isomorphic to a subgroup of $\Sigma_k\wr U(m)$ for some $k\geq 1$.
  This global class is multiplicative because $(\Sigma_k\wr U(m))\times (\Sigma_l\wr U(m))$
  embeds into  $\Sigma_{k+l}\wr U(m)$.
  And ${\mathcal F}_m$ is closed under wreath products because
  $\Sigma_k\wr(\Sigma_l\wr U(m))$ embeds into  $\Sigma_{k l}\wr U(m)$.
  By design, ${\mathcal F}_m$ is the minimal multiplicative global class that contains $U(m)$
  and is closed under wreath products.

  We let $\delta\colon L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$ be an ${\mathcal F}_m$-approximation
  of the global $K$-theory spectrum in the $\infty$-category $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$
  of ultra-commutative ring spectra, in the sense of Remark \ref{rk:approxFucom}.
  So this morphism is terminal in the full subcategory of $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}/{\mathbf{KU}}$
  spanned by morphisms whose source is ${\mathcal F}_m$-left induced as a global spectrum.
  Such a morphism exists by Theorem \ref{thm:wreath_closed} (iv).
  
  Since ${\mathbf P}$ is a global classifying space of
  the abelian compact Lie group $U(1)$,
  the global spectrum $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ is left induced from the
  global family ${\mathcal A}b$ of abelian compact Lie groups.
  Hence $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ is also left induced from the larger global class ${\mathcal F}_m$.
  So the morphism $\eta\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$ factors uniquely
  as a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra $\psi\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$
  followed by $\delta\colon L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$.
  Since $\delta$ is an ${\mathcal F}_m$-equivalence, since $U(m)\in{\mathcal F}_m$,
  and since $\eta$ inverts $b_m$, the morphism
  $\psi\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$ also inverts $b_m$.
  We will show that $\psi$ does {\em not} invert $b_{m+1}$.
  Incidentally, for $m=1$ the family ${\mathcal F}_1$ is the family ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$
  of compact Lie groups with abelian identity component, and we show in
  Theorem \ref{thm:ucom b_1 loc} below that the morphism
  $\psi\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal A}b^\circ}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$ is an ultra-commutative
  localization by $b_1$. For $m\geq 2$, I do not know whether
  $\psi\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$ is an ultra-commutative
  localization by $b_m$.
  
  To show that $\psi\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$ does not invert $b_{m+1}$
  we consider the group $S U(m+1)$. 
  Since $S U(m+1)$ is connected, every continuous homomorphism
  from $S U(m+1)$ to $\Sigma_k\wr U(m)$ takes values in the identity component
  $U(m)^k$ of the target.
  Since every nontrivial irreducible $S U(m+1)$-representation
  has dimension at least $m+1$, any such homomorphism is trivial.
  Hence the unique homomorphism $p_{SU(m+1)}\colon S U(m+1)\longrightarrow\{1\}$
  is initial among morphisms from $S U(m+1)$ to groups in ${\mathcal F}_m$.
  Since $L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$ is  ${\mathcal F}_m$-left induced,
  and since this global class is multiplicative,
  the inflation homomorphism
  \[ p_{S U(m+1)}^*\ : \ \pi_0(L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})) =
    \Phi_0^{\{1\}}(L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})) \ \longrightarrow \ \Phi^{S U(m+1)}_0(L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})) \]
  is an isomorphism by Proposition \ref{prop:reflexive} (ii).
  Because $L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$ is non-equivariantly equivalent to ${\mathbf{KU}}$,
  the source ring $\pi_0(L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}}))$ is isomorphic to $\pi_0({\mathbf{KU}})={\mathbb Z}$.
  We conclude that $\Phi^{S U(m+1)}_0(L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}}))\allowbreak\cong{\mathbb Z}$.
  Since $SU(m+1)$ is connected, it has no proper closed subgroups of finite index. 
  So the tautological $S U(m+1)$-representation $\nu_{m+1}$
  is not induced from any 1-dimensional representation of a closed subgroup of $S U(m+1)$,
  and we obtain the relation
  \[ \Phi^{S U(m+1)}(\operatorname{res}^{U(m+1)}_{S U(m+1)}(b_{m+1}))\ = \
    \Phi^{S U(m+1)}(b_{S U(m+1),\nu_{m+1}})\ =\ 0\]
  in $\Phi^{S U(m+1)}_0(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$, by Theorem \ref{thm:Phi_on_irrep}.
  If $\psi_*(b_{m+1})$ were invertible in $L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$,
  then  $\psi_*(\Phi^{S U(m+1)}\allowbreak(b_{S U(m+1),\nu_{m+1}}))=0$
  would be invertible in the ring $\Phi_0^{S U(m+1)}(L_{{\mathcal F}_m}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}}))$,
  contradicting the fact that this ring is nontrivial.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:glcom b_1 loc}
    The morphism of commutative global ring spectra
    $\eta^\natural\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})$
    is a global localization in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$
    by the pre-Bott class $b_1$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
We let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  The projection $q_G\colon G\longrightarrow G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ to the abelianization is initial among continuous
  homomorphisms to abelian compact Lie groups;
  so the global family ${\mathcal A}b$ is reflexive in the sense of \cite[Definition 4.5.7]{schwede:global}.
  The underlying global spectra of both $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ and $L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})$
  are left induced from the global family ${\mathcal A}b$.
  So \cite[Proposition 4.5.8]{schwede:global} shows that both vertical inflation morphisms
  in the commutative square of graded-commutative rings
  \[ \xymatrix@C=18mm{\Phi_*^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[d]^\cong_{q_G^*}
      \ar[r]_-{\Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}_*(\eta^\natural)}\ar@/^2pc/[rr]^(.2){\Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}_*(\eta)}&
      \Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}_*(L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}}))\ar[d]^{q_G^*}_\cong \ar[r]^-{\cong}_-{\Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}_*(\epsilon)}&
      \Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}_*({\mathbf{KU}})\\
      \Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]_-{\Phi^G_*(\eta^\natural)} &
      \Phi^G_*(L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}}))
    } \]
  are isomorphisms, see also Proposition \ref{prop:reflexive}.
  By Theorem \ref{thm:geomfix}, the morphism $\Phi_*^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}(\eta)$
  is a localization by the classes $\Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}(b_{G_{\operatorname{ab}},V})$
  for all unitary $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$-representations $V$.
  Since  $\epsilon\colon L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$ is an ${\mathcal A}b$-equivalence,
  it induces an isomorphism of $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$-geometric fixed points, and so
  also the morphism $\Phi_*^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}(\eta^\natural)$
  is a localization by the same classes.
  Since $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$ is abelian, every $G_{\operatorname{ab}}$-representation is a direct sum
  of 1-dimensional representations. By the multiplicativity of the pre-Bott classes
  (Theorem \ref{thm:fix of pre-Bott} (ii)),
  the morphism $\Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}_*(\eta^\natural)$ is also 
  a localization by the classes $\Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}(b_{G_{\operatorname{ab}},\chi})$
  for all continuous homomorphisms $\chi\colon G_{\operatorname{ab}}\longrightarrow T$.
  Since $q_G^*(\Phi^{G_{\operatorname{ab}}}(b_{G_{\operatorname{ab}},\chi}))= \Phi^G(b_{G,\chi\circ q_G})$,
  and since every continuous homomorphism $G\longrightarrow T$ factors uniquely through
  $q_G\colon G\longrightarrow G_{\operatorname{ab}}$, this shows that the lower horizontal morphism  $\Phi^G_*(\eta^\natural)$
  is a localization by the classes $\Phi^G(b_{G,\alpha})=\Phi^G(\alpha^*(b_1))$
  for all continuous homomorphisms $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow T$.
  The geometric fixed point criterion of Theorem \ref{thm:fix_criterion}
  applied to the single class $b_1$ thus shows that
  $\eta^\natural\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})$
  is a global localization by $b_1$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:ucom b_1 loc}
    The morphism
    $\eta^\flat\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P} \longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal A}b^\circ}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$
    is an ultra-commutative localization by the pre-Bott class $b_1$.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
In a first step we show the following claim:
  For every group $G$ in the global family ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$,
  the morphism of geometric fixed point rings
  \[ \Phi^G_*(\eta)\ : \ \Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \longrightarrow \ \Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}}) \]
  is a localization by the set of classes $\Phi^G(\beta^*(P^m(b_1)))$
  for all $m\geq 1$ and all continuous homomorphisms $\beta\colon G\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr T$.

  We start with the case where $G$ is cyclic.
  Then all irreducible unitary $G$-representations are 1-dimensional.
  Hence in this case the morphism
  $\Phi^G_*(\eta)\colon\Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})$
  is a localization by the set of classes $\Phi^G(b_{G,\chi})=\Phi^G(\chi^*(b_1))$
  for all continuous homomorphisms $\chi\colon G\longrightarrow T$,
  by Theorem \ref{thm:geomfix}. Since $\eta$ is a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra,
  it is compatible with geometric fixed points, restrictions, and power operations,
  and each of these operations preserves invertibility
  by Propositions  \ref{prop:invert_criterion},  \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert},
  and \ref{prop:invertibility_power}, respectively.
  Since $\eta_*(b_1)$ is invertible by Theorem \ref{thm:pre-Bott}, the classes 
  \[  \eta_*(\Phi^G(\beta^*(P^m(b_1)))) \ = \ \Phi^G(\beta^*(P^m(\eta_*(b_1)))) \]
  are all invertible in $\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})$ for all $m\geq 2$.
  Hence these classes are already invertible after inverting the
  classes for $m=1$, and thus $\Phi^G_*(\eta)$ is also a localization by the larger set.

  Now we assume that $G$ is in the family ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$, but it is not cyclic.
  We claim that then $G$ has at least one of the following two properties:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item[(A)] The group $G$ admits a continuous epimorphism onto $C_p\times C_p$ for some prime $p$.
  \item[(B)] There is a finite index subgroup $H$ of $G$ and a nontrivial
    character $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$ such that $\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)=1$.
  \end{itemize}

  If the component group $\pi_0(G)$ is cyclic, then $G$ must be nonabelian,
  for else $G$ would be cyclic.
  Theorem \ref{thm:G^circ_image} (ii) then provides the data $(H,\chi)$
  witnessing that $G$ has property (B).

  If the component group $\pi_0(G)$ is not cyclic, then
  $\pi_0(G)$ admits a homomorphism onto a near-cyclic group in the sense of 
  Definition \ref{def:near-cyclic}.
  So there is a continuous epimorphism $\epsilon\colon G\longrightarrow K$
  onto a finite near-cyclic group.
  This near-cyclic group $K$ has one of the properties (a), (b) or (c)
  listed in Proposition \ref{prop:nearcyclic}.
  The groups in class (a) are of the form $C_p\times C_p$ for some prime $p$;
  so if $K$ has property (a), then $G$ has property (A).

  If $K$ has property (b) or (c), then
  the addendum of Proposition \ref{prop:nearcyclic}
  provides a subgroup $L$ of $K$ and a nontrivial character $\lambda\colon L\longrightarrow T$
  such that $\operatorname{tr}_L^K(\lambda)=1$.
  Then $H=\epsilon^{-1}(L)$ is a finite index subgroup of $G$, and
  $\chi=\lambda\circ \epsilon|_H\colon H\longrightarrow T$ is a nontrivial character such that
  \[ \operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)\ = \
    \operatorname{tr}_H^G(\lambda\circ\epsilon|_H)\ = \ \operatorname{tr}_L^K(\lambda)\circ\epsilon \ = \ 1\ .\]
  So $G$ has property (B).

  If $G$ has property (A), we let $\epsilon\colon G\longrightarrow C_p\times C_p$ be an epimorphism, 
  for some prime $p$. The relation
  \[ \prod_{\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}(C_p\times C_p,T)\setminus\{1\}}(1-\lambda) \ = \ 0 \]
  holds in the integral group ring ${\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(C_p\times C_p,T)]$,
  where the product is over the $p^2-1$ nontrivial characters of $C_p\times C_p$.  
  Hence the relation
  \[ \prod_{\lambda\in\operatorname{Hom}(C_p\times C_p,T)\setminus\{1\}}(1-(\lambda\circ\epsilon)) \ = \ 0 \]
  holds in the group ring ${\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)]$, and the $G$-characters $\lambda\circ\epsilon$
  that occur are all nontrivial.
  In the ring $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\cong {\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)]$,
  we are in particular inverting the classes
  \[ \Phi^G((\lambda\circ\epsilon)^*(b_1))\ = \ \Phi^G(b_{G,\lambda\circ\epsilon})\ = _{\eqref{eq:Phi^G_of_char}}\ 1 -(\lambda\circ\epsilon)^\sharp\ , \]
  and hence also their product.
  So the relevant localization of  $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  is the zero ring, consistent with the fact that $\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})=0$ for non-cyclic groups $G$.
  
  If $G$ has property (B), witnessed by $(H,\chi)$, then 
  we set $\beta=(\Sigma_m\wr\chi)\circ\Psi_{\bar g}\colon G\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr T$,
  where $m=[G:H]$, and $\Psi_{\bar g}\colon G\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr H$  
  is the monomorphism  \eqref{eq:define_Psi} arising from a choice of transversal
  of $H$ in $G$.
  Then
  \begin{align*}
    \Phi^G(\beta^*(P^m(b_1)))\
    &= \ \Phi^G(\Psi^*_{\bar g}((\Sigma_m\wr\chi)^*(P^m(b_1))))\
    = \ \Phi^G(\Psi^*_{\bar g}(P^m(\chi^*(b_1))))\\
    &= \ \Phi^G(\Psi^*_{\bar g}(P^m(b_{H,\chi})))\  = \ 1- \operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)^\sharp\ = \ 0 \ . 
  \end{align*}
  The second equality  $(\Sigma_m\wr\chi)^*\circ P^m=P^m\circ\chi^*$
  is naturality of the power operation with respect to restriction along group homomorphisms;
  the proof is straightforward from the definitions.
  The fourth equality is Proposition \ref{prop:monomial_basis} (iv).
  So the localization of $\Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$ by 
  $\Phi^G(\beta^*(P^m(b_1)))$ is the zero ring, consistent with the
  fact that $\Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})$ is trivial for non-cyclic groups $G$.

  With the claim established, we now show that
  the underlying morphism in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$
  of $\eta^\flat\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\allowbreak\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal A}b^\circ}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$
  is a global localization by the set of classes $\{P^m(b_1)\}_{m\geq 1}$.
  The global family ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$ is multiplicative, and hence reflexive
  by Proposition \ref{prop:mult=refl}, i.e., the inclusion of ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$
  into all compact Lie groups has a left adjoint.
  For a compact Lie group $G$,
  the initial homomorphism $p\colon G\longrightarrow G_\diamond$ to a group in ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$ is the projection
  onto the quotient group  $G_\diamond=G/(G^\circ)'$, where $(G^\circ)'=[G^\circ,G^\circ]$
  is the commutator subgroup of the identity component $G^\circ$ of $G$. 

  Both $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ and $L_{{\mathcal A}b^\circ}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}})$
  are left induced from the global family ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$.
  So \cite[Proposition 4.5.8]{schwede:global}
  or Proposition \ref{prop:reflexive} (ii) show that both vertical inflation morphisms
  in the commutative square of graded-commutative rings
  \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\label{eq:G_diamond}
 \xymatrix@C=15mm{\Phi_*^{G_{\diamond}}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})
      \ar[d]^\cong_{p^*}\ar@/^2pc/[rr]^(.2){\Phi^{G_\diamond}_*(\eta)}
      \ar[r]_-{\Phi^{G_\diamond}_*(\eta^\flat)}&
      \Phi^{G_\diamond}_*(L_{{\mathcal A}b^\circ}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}}))\ar[d]_\cong^{p^*}
      \ar[r]_-{\Phi^{G_\diamond}_*(\delta)}^\cong &      \Phi^{G_\diamond}_*({\mathbf{KU}}) \\
      \Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]_-{\Phi^G_*(\eta^\flat)}
      &  \Phi^G_*(L_{{\mathcal A}b^\circ}^{\operatorname{uc}}({\mathbf{KU}}))
    }     \end{aligned}  \end{equation}
  are isomorphisms. The right upper horizontal map is an isomorphism because
  $\delta$ is an ${\mathcal A}b^\circ$-equivalence.
  
  By the above claim applied to $G_\diamond$,
  the morphism $\Phi_*^{G_\diamond}(\eta)$ is a localization by the set of classes
  \[ \Phi^{G_\diamond}(\beta^*(P^m(b_1))) \]
  for all $m\geq 1$ and all continuous homomorphisms $\beta\colon G_\diamond\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr T$.
  The commutative diagram \eqref{eq:G_diamond} thus shows that the lower horizontal homomorphism
  $\Phi^G_*(\eta^\flat)$ is a localization by the set of classes
  \[    p^*(\Phi^{G_\diamond}(\beta^*(P^m(b_1)))) \ = \
    \Phi^G(p^*(\beta^*(P^m(b_1))))\ = \   \Phi^G((\beta\circ p)^*(P^m(b_1)))
  \]
  for the same set of pairs $(m,\beta)$.
  Every continuous homomorphism $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr T$
  annihilates $(G^\circ)'$,
  and hence factors uniquely as $\alpha=\beta\circ p$ for
  a continuous homomorphism $\beta\colon G_\diamond\longrightarrow \Sigma_m\wr T$.
  So  $\Phi^G_*(\eta^\flat)$ is also a localization by the set of classes
  $\Phi^G(\alpha^*(P^m(b_1)))$ for all $m\geq 1$ and all
  continuous homomorphisms $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr T$.
  The geometric fixed point criterion of Theorem \ref{thm:fix_criterion}
  thus proves the claim that $\eta^\flat$  is a global localization in
  $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}})$ by the set $\{P^m(b_1)\}_{m\geq 1}$.

  Since $\eta^\flat$ arises as a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra,
  and since the underlying morphism is a global localization in
  $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}})$ by $\{P^m(b_1)\}_{m\geq 1}$,
  Theorem \ref{thm:UR2CR} (iii) shows that $\eta^\flat$
  is also an ultra-commutative localization by $\{P^m(b_1)\}_{m\geq 1}$ in
  the more highly structured category $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$.
  A morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra $j\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow S$
  is compatible with power operations, and thus inverts the class $b_1$
  if and only if it inverts $P^m(b_1)$ for all $m\geq 1$,
  compare Proposition \ref{prop:invertibility_power}.
  So every ultra-commutative localization in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$ by $b_1$
  is also an ultra-commutative localization by $\{P^m(b_1)\}_{m\geq 1}$,
  and vice versa.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- eg-5: body_md -->
\label{eg:Sigma_3_witnesses}
  We will now show that the commutative global ring spectrum $L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})$
  does not underlie any ultra-commutative ring spectrum.
  We argue by contradiction and suppose that there was an ultra-commutative ring spectrum $R$
  and an equivalence $s\colon L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})\xrightarrow{\sim}u_{\operatorname{gl}}(R)$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}})$.
  We let $\zeta\colon A_3\longrightarrow T$ denote either of the two nontrivial characters of the
  alternating group $A_3$.
  If $\eta^\natural\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})$
  denotes the global localization by $b_1$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$
  discussed in Theorem \ref{thm:glcom b_1 loc},
  then the class 
  \[ B_{A_3,\zeta}\ =\ (s\circ \eta^\natural)_*(b_{A_3,\zeta}) \ = \
    s_*(\zeta^*(\eta^\natural_*(b_1)))\]
  in $\pi_\zeta^{A_3}(R)$ is invertible  by
  Propositions \ref{prop:invert_inherit} (i) and \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert}.
  Since $R$ is ultra-commutative, the class
  $\Phi^{\Sigma_3}(\Psi^*(P^2(B_{A_3,\zeta})))$ is then invertible by
  Propositions \ref{prop:invert_criterion},
  \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert} and \ref{prop:invertibility_power}.
  
  We set $x=(s\circ\eta^\natural)_*(\zeta^*(e_T))\in\pi_0^{A_3}(R)$;
  then $x^3=1$, because $\zeta^3=1$.
  Moreover,
  \[ i^*(B_{A_3,\zeta})\ = \ (s\circ\eta^\natural)_*(i^*(b_{A_3,\zeta}))\ =_{\eqref{eq:i^*_of_b}}  \
    (s\circ\eta^\natural)_*(1-\zeta^*(e_T))\ = \ 1-x \ , \]
  for $i\colon S^0\longrightarrow S^{\zeta}$ the fixed point inclusion.
  
  We let $\Psi\colon\Sigma_3\longrightarrow\Sigma_2\wr A_3$ be the monomorphism \eqref{eq:define_Psi}
  based on some transversal of the alternating group $A_3$ in $\Sigma_3$.
  We showed in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:monomial_basis} (iv)
  that the map
  \[  N\ =\ \Phi^{\Sigma_3}\circ\Psi^*\circ P^2\ \colon\ \pi_0^{A_3}(R)\ \longrightarrow \
    \Phi_0^{\Sigma_3}(R) \]
  is additive, and hence a unital ring homomorphism.
  The hypotheses provide ring isomorphisms
  \[ \Phi_0^{\Sigma_3}(R)\ \cong\ \Phi_0^{\Sigma_3}(L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}}))\ \cong\ \Phi_0^{C_2}(L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}}))\ \cong
    \  \Phi_0^{C_2}({\mathbf{KU}}) \ \cong  \   {\mathbb Z}[1/2]\ .\]
  The second isomorphism is by inflation along the quotient map
  $\Sigma_3\longrightarrow C_2$ to the abelianization, using Proposition \ref{prop:reflexive} (ii).
  The third uses that $C_2$ belongs to the family ${\mathcal A}b$.
  The only cube root of unity in ${\mathbb Z}[1/2]$, and hence in $\Phi^{\Sigma_3}_0(R)$,
  is 1, so $N(x)=1$.
  Then
  \begin{align*}
    \Phi^{\Sigma_3}(\Psi^*(P^2(B_{A_3,\zeta})))\
    &= \ \Phi^{\Sigma_3}(\bar i^*(\Psi^*(P^2(B_{A_3,\zeta}))))\
      = \ N(i^*(B_{A_3,\zeta}))\  = \ N(1-x)\  =\  0\ ,
  \end{align*}
  where now $\bar i$ is the inclusion of $\Sigma_3$-fixed points
  $S^0\longrightarrow S^{\operatorname{ind}_{A_3}^{\Sigma_3}(\zeta)}$.
  We conclude that 0 is a unit in $\Phi_0^{\Sigma_3}(R)\cong{\mathbb Z}[1/2]$, which is a contradiction.
  So $L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})$ does not underlie any ultra-commutative ring spectrum.
  By Theorem \ref{thm:glcom b_1 loc},
  $L_{{\mathcal A}b}({\mathbf{KU}})$ is the commutative global localization of $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ by $b_1$;
  so in particular, the commutative global localization and
  the ultra-commutative localization of $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ by $b_1$ are not equivalent.
<!-- end eg-5 -->
<!-- construction-13: body_md -->
A morphism $f\colon X\longrightarrow Y$ of orthogonal $C$-spectra is a {\em $C$-global equivalence}
if for every augmented Lie group $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow C$ and all integers $k$, the map
$\pi_k^G(\alpha^*(f))\colon\pi_k^G(\alpha^*(X))\longrightarrow \pi_k^G(\alpha^*(Y))$ is an isomorphism.
The $C$-global equivalences are the weak equivalences
in a stable model structure on the category $\operatorname{Sp}^O_C$ of orthogonal $C$-spectra,
which is moreover symmetric monoidal with cofibrant unit for the smash product,
see \cite{grande:MA}, or Theorem 7.8 and Corollary 7.19 of \cite{brink-lenz}.
The monoidal localization thus yields a symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category
  \[ {\mathcal S} p^{\wedge}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}} \ = \ (\operatorname{Sp}^{O,\wedge}_C)_\infty \]
  and a lax symmetric monoidal functor
  \[ \gamma_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}^\wedge \ : \ \operatorname{Sp}^{O,\wedge}_C\  \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S} p^{\wedge}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}} \]
  whose underlying functor
  is a localization of the 1-category of orthogonal $C$-spectra at the class
  of $C$-global equivalences.
  We refer to the underlying $\infty$-category ${\mathcal S} p_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$
  as the {\em $\infty$-category of $C$-global spectra};
  it is stable and compactly generated,
  and hence presentable, by \cite[Corollary A.19]{schwede:stiefel}.
  The monoidal product on ${\mathcal S} p^{\wedge}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$ arises from a Quillen bifunctor
  at the level of the model, and so it preserves colimits in each variable;
  hence  ${\mathcal S} p^{\wedge}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$ is presentably symmetric monoidal.
  The $\infty$-category $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}})$ of {\em commutative $C$-global ring spectra}
  is thus presentable by \cite[Corollary 3.2.3.5]{lurie:higher_algebra}.
<!-- end construction-13 -->
<!-- construction-14: body_md -->
In Construction \ref{con:res_G} we introduce the `underlying $G$-spectrum functor'
  from global spectra to $G$-spectra, for any compact Lie group $G$.
  In the $C$-global context, every augmented Lie group $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow C$
  gives rise to an analogous functor, as follows.
  The 1-categorical restriction functor
  \[ \alpha^* \ : \ \operatorname{Sp}^O_C\ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{Sp}_G^O \ , \quad X \ \longmapsto \ \alpha^*(X) \]
  from orthogonal $C$-spectra to orthogonal $G$-spectra
  takes $C$-global equivalences to ${\underline \pi}_*$-isomorphisms, by definition.
  And this restriction functor is strong symmetric monoidal
  for the respective smash products, with diagonal action.
  The universal property of the monoidal localization
  $\gamma^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}\colon \operatorname{Sp}_C^{O,\wedge}\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}^\wedge$
  yields a unique lax symmetric monoidal functor
  \[  \operatorname{res}_\alpha^{\wedge} \ : \ {\mathcal S} p_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}^{\wedge} \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S} p_G^{\wedge}     \]
  equipped with a monoidal equivalence
  \[ \gamma_G^\wedge\circ \alpha^* \ \sim \ \operatorname{res}_\alpha^\wedge \circ \gamma^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}\ \colon\
   \operatorname{Sp}^{O,\wedge}_C\ \longrightarrow \  {\mathcal S} p_G^{\wedge} \ . \]
 The same kind of argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:gl2G} (iv)
 shows that the a priori only lax symmetric monoidal functor $\operatorname{res}_\alpha^{\wedge}$
 is in fact strong.
<!-- end construction-14 -->
<!-- defn-7: body_md -->
Let $R$ be a commutative $C$-global ring spectrum.
  A {\em set of representation-graded equivariant homotopy classes} of $R$
  is a set ${\mathcal X}=\{v\}$ of
  classes in $\pi_V^\alpha(R)$ for varying pairs $(\alpha,V)$ consisting
  of an augmented Lie group $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow C$ and a $G$-representation $V$.
  We will say that the class $v\in \pi_V^\alpha(R)$ is {\em supported}
  at the homomorphism $\alpha$, or at the pair $(\alpha,V)$.
  A morphism $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ of commutative $C$-global ring spectra
  {\em inverts ${\mathcal X}$} if for every
  element $v\in{\mathcal X}$ supported at $(\alpha,V)$, the class $\pi_V^\alpha(i)(v)\in\pi_V^\alpha(S)$
  is invertible in the sense of Definition \ref{def:RO-invertible}.
  A {\em $C$-global localization by ${\mathcal X}$}
  is an initial object of the full subcategory of the
  slice category $R\backslash\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}^\wedge)$ spanned by the
  ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms.
<!-- end defn-7 -->
<!-- construction-15: body_md -->
\label{con:Real pre-Bott}  
  We write $\tilde T=T\rtimes C$ for the {\em extended circle group},
  the semidirect product of the group $C=\operatorname{Gal}({\mathbb C}/{\mathbb R})$
  acting by complex conjugation on $T=U(1)$.
  The group $\tilde T$ is augmented to $C$ by the projection.
  We abuse notation and write $\nu_1$ for the tautological Real
  $\tilde T$-representation on ${\mathbb C}$ by scalar multiplication and complex conjugation.
  The underlying unitary $T$-representation of $\nu_1$ is the tautological
  representation with the same name, justifying the abuse.
  We introduce a {\em Real-global pre-Bott class} $\tilde b_1$
  in the $\tilde T$-equivariant homotopy group of $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$
  that restricts to the first pre-Bott class from Construction \ref{con:pre-Bott}  
  on the underlying `non-Real' global spectrum.

  We embed the group $C$ into $\tilde T$ as complex conjugation.
  The cofiber sequence of based $\tilde T$-spaces
\[  \tilde T/C_+ \ \longrightarrow \ S^0 \ \xrightarrow{\ i \ } \ S^{\nu_1}  \]
  induces a long exact sequence in any $\tilde T$-equivariant cohomology theory.
  For $C$-global spectra, the restriction homomorphism $\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C$
  is a split epimorphism, by inflation along the augmentation $\tilde T\longrightarrow C$;
  so the long exact sequence splits off
  a short exact sequence:
  \[ \xymatrix@C=9mm{
      0\ar[r] & \pi_{\nu_1}^{\tilde T}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]^-{i^*} &
      \pi_0^{\tilde T}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]^-{\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C}&
      \pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r] & 0     } \]
  We alert the reader that according to our present conventions,
  here and below the group $C$ is augmented by the identity,
  so it acts on $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ by complex conjugation.
  This is {\em different} from the trivial $C$-action,
  which occurs for example in Proposition \ref{prop:modulo_torsion}.
  We write $e_{\tilde T}\in \pi_0^{\tilde T}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ for the stable tautological class,
  see \cite[(4.2)]{schwede:GSB};
  its restriction to $T$ is the tautological class $e_T$ from \eqref{eq:define_e_T}.
  The ring $\pi_0^C(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ is isomorphic to the Burnside ring of the group $C$,
  and additively generated by $1=\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(e_{\tilde T})$,
  the multiplicative unit, and the class $\operatorname{tr}_{\{1\}}^C(1)=\operatorname{tr}_{\{1\}}^C(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_{\{1\}}(e_{\tilde T}))$.
  Because $\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(1- e_{\tilde T})=0$,
  there is a unique class, the {\em Real-global pre-Bott class}
  \[  \tilde b_1 \ \in \ \pi_{\nu_1}^{\tilde T}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}) \text{\quad such that\quad}
    i^*(\tilde b_1)\ = \ 1- e_{\tilde T}\text{\quad in\quad} \pi_0^{\tilde T}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ . \]
<!-- end construction-15 -->
<!-- prop-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:properties_tilde b}\ 
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item
    The relation $\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T(\tilde b_1)=b_1$ holds in $\pi^T_{\nu_1}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
  \item
    The morphism $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KR}}$
    sends the class $\tilde b_1$ to the $\tilde T$-equivariant Bott class of $\nu_1$.      
  \item
    The class $\Phi^C(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(\tilde b_1))$ in $\Phi^C_1(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
    is nilpotent, where $C$ sits inside $\tilde T$ as complex conjugation. 
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-12 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
(i) By design we have
  \[ i^*(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T(\tilde b_1))\ = \
    \operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T(i^*(\tilde b_1))\ = \
    \operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T(1-e_{\tilde T})\ = \   1-e_T \ = \ i^*(b_1)  \]
  in the group $\pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$. Since the map
  $i^*\colon\pi_{\nu_1}^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  is injective, this proves the desired relation.

  (ii)
  The forgetful ring homomorphism $\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T\colon RR(\tilde T)\longrightarrow RU (T)$
  from the Real representation ring of $\tilde T$
  is injective by \cite[page 13]{atiyah-segal:completion}.
  By Real-equivariant Bott periodicity \cite[Theorem 5.1]{atiyah:elliptic},
  the restriction homomorphism
  $\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T\colon \pi_{\nu_1}^{\tilde T}({\mathbf{KR}})\longrightarrow\pi_{\nu_1}^T({\mathbf{KR}})$
  is then injective, too. 
  It also takes the $\tilde T$-equivariant Bott class $\beta_{\tilde T,\nu_1}$
  to the $T$-equivariant Bott class $\beta_{T,\nu_1}$.
  Since $\eta$ is a morphism of $C$-global spectra, we have
  \[ \operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T(\eta_*(\tilde b_1))\ = \
    \eta_*(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T(\tilde b_1))\ = \
    \eta_*(b_1)\ = \ \beta_{T,\nu_1} \ = \ \operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T(\beta_{\tilde T,\nu_1})\ , \]
  where the third equation is Remark \ref{rk:preBott2Bott}.
  Since $\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_T$ is injective,
  the desired relation $\eta_*(\tilde b_1)=\beta_{\tilde T,\nu_1}$ follows.

  (iii) The underlying $C$-space of the $C$-global space ${\mathbf P}$
  is infinite complex projective space with $C$-action by complex conjugation.
  So the fixed point space ${\mathbf P}^C$ is homeomorphic to ${\mathbb R} P^\infty$.
  The geometric fixed point groups of an equivariant suspension spectrum
  are isomorphic to the stable homotopy groups of the fixed point space,
  compare \cite[Example 3.3.3]{schwede:global}. So the ring $\Phi^C_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  is isomorphic to $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbb R} P^\infty)$.
  The non-equivariant stable homotopy groups of ${\mathbb R} P^\infty$
  are explicitly known in small degrees, see for example \cite{liulevicius}.
  In particular, $\pi_5(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbb R} P^\infty)=0$,
  so the fifth power of every class in $\pi_1(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbb R} P^\infty)$ is zero.
  Hence also the fifth power of the class $\Phi^C(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(\tilde b_1))$ is zero.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:Realglobal}\
  The morphism $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KR}}$
  is a $C$-global localization in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}^\wedge)$
  by the classes $\tilde b_1$ and $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 2}$.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
We apply the localization recognition of Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg}
  to the presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category ${\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$
  of $C$-global spectra, to the morphism $\eta\colon\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KR}}$,
  and to the family of geometric fixed point functors
  $\Phi^G\circ\operatorname{res}^\wedge_\alpha\colon{\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p^\wedge$,
  for $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow C$ ranging
  through representatives of all isomorphism classes of augmented Lie groups.
  These functors are strong symmetric monoidal left adjoints, and jointly conservative,
  by the $C$-global analog of Theorem \ref{thm:gl2G}.
  The full subcategory ${\mathcal W}$ of $(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\backslash\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}})$
  is spanned by the morphisms that invert the pre-Bott classes $\tilde b_1$ and $b_m$ for $m\geq 2$.
  It is closed under postcomposition by the $C$-global analog of
  Proposition \ref{prop:invert_inherit} (i).
  The morphism $\eta\colon\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KR}}$ inverts $\tilde b_1$ by
  Proposition \ref{prop:properties_tilde b} (ii) and Real-equivariant Bott periodicity
  \cite[Theorem 5.1]{atiyah:elliptic};
  and it inverts the classes $b_m$ by Theorem \ref{thm:pre-Bott}.
  
  Now we verify hypothesis (c) for an augmented Lie group $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow C$.
  If the augmentation $\alpha$ is trivial, then ${\mathbf{KR}}_\alpha={\mathbf{KU}}_G$,
  and similarly for $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$. So in this case, the morphism of graded rings
  $\Phi^\alpha_*(\eta)\colon\Phi^\alpha_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \Phi^\alpha_*({\mathbf{KR}})$
  specializes to $\Phi^G_*(\eta)\colon\Phi^G_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \Phi^G_*({\mathbf{KU}})$,
  with the understanding that now $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$ and ${\mathbf{KU}}$
  denote the underlying global spectra.
  This homomorphism is a localization by the set of classes $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})$
  for all unitary $G$-representations $V$, by Theorem \ref{thm:geomfix}.
  Moreover, if $f\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow P$ belongs to ${\mathcal W}$,
  then it inverts $b_m$ for all $m\geq 1$; for $m=1$, this is because $f$ inverts
  $\tilde b_1$, and hence also its restriction $b_1$.
  So $f$ inverts all the classes $\Phi^G(b_{G,V})$, by 
  Propositions \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert} and \ref{prop:invert_criterion}.
  Since $\Phi^G_*(\eta)$ is a localization by these classes, the morphism $\Phi^G_*(f)$
  factors through $\Phi^G_*(\eta)$. This verifies hypothesis (c) for trivial augmentations.

  If the augmentation $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow C$ is surjective, then the inflation homomorphism
  $\alpha^*\colon\Phi^C_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \Phi^\alpha_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  is a ring homomorphism. Since $\Phi^C(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(\tilde b_1))$ is nilpotent
  by Proposition \ref{prop:properties_tilde b} (iii), also the class
  \[ \Phi^\alpha_*(f)(\alpha^*(\Phi^C(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(\tilde b_1)))) \ =\
    \Phi^G(\alpha^*(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(f_*(\tilde b_1)))) \]
  is nilpotent. Because $f\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow P$ inverts $\tilde b_1$,
  it also inverts $\alpha^*(\Phi^C(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(\tilde b_1)))$ by 
  Propositions \ref{prop:invert_criterion} and \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert}. 
  So $\Phi^G(\alpha^*(\operatorname{res}^{\tilde T}_C(f_*(\tilde b_1))))$ is both nilpotent
  and invertible, and the commutative ring spectrum $\Phi^\alpha(P)$ is trivial.
  In particular, the ring spectrum $\Phi^\alpha({\mathbf{KR}})$ is trivial.
  So $\Phi^\alpha_*(\eta)\colon\Phi^\alpha_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \Phi^\alpha_*({\mathbf{KR}})$
  is a localization, namely the effect of inverting 0.
  And $\Phi^\alpha_*(f)\colon \Phi^\alpha_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\Phi^\alpha_*(P)$
  factors through $\Phi^\alpha_*(\eta)$, proving (c).  
  So altogether, Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg} applies
  and shows that $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KR}}$
  is a $C$-global localization by $\{\tilde b_1, b_m\mid m\geq 2\}$
  in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}})$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- rk-10: body_md -->
\label{rk:C_global_UCom}
  The $\infty$-category of {\em ultra-commutative $C$-global ring spectra} $\operatorname{URing}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$
  is the localization of the 1-category of commutative orthogonal $C$-ring spectra
  at the class of $C$-global equivalences.
  I expect that the $C$-global equivalences on the category of
  commutative orthogonal $C$-ring spectra are the weak equivalences in
  a model structure that generalizes the global model structure
  for ultra-commutative ring spectra from \cite[Theorem 5.4.3]{schwede:global}.
  Granted this, we could deduce that the $\infty$-category $\operatorname{URing}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$ is
  complete and cocomplete.

  Let $R$ be an ultra-commutative $C$-global ring spectrum, and
  let ${\mathcal X}$ be a set of representation-graded equivariant homotopy classes of $R$.
  An {\em ultra-commutative $C$-global localization by ${\mathcal X}$}
  is an initial object of the full subcategory of the
  slice category $R\backslash \operatorname{URing}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$ spanned by the ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms.
  I expect that the morphism $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KR}}$
  is an ultra-commutative $C$-global localization
  by the classes $\tilde b_1$ and $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 2}$.
  In fact, the entire proof of the non-Real counterpart in 
  Theorem \ref{thm:main} (ii) should generalize to the Real-global context, as follows.
 
  Much like in \eqref{eq:ucom2CR_gl}, we obtain a `forgetful' functor
  \[ u_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}\ :\ \operatorname{URing}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}\ \longrightarrow\  \operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}})  \]
  from the $\infty$-category of ultra-commutative $C$-global ring spectra to the
  $\infty$-category of commutative $C$-global ring spectra.
  Theorem \ref{thm:UR_monadic} should generalize, hopefully with
  essentially the same proof, to show that the $\infty$-category $\operatorname{URing}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$
  is presentable and that the functor $u_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$ is bimonadic.
  Granted this, in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:UR2CR},
  we could replace `global' by `$C$-global' throughout, and replace compact Lie groups
  by augmented compact Lie groups.
  We would then in particular obtain the following $C$-global generalization of
  Theorem \ref{thm:UR2CR} (iii):
  let $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ be a morphism of ultra-commutative $C$-global ring spectra, and
  let ${\mathcal X}$ be a set of representation-graded equivariant homotopy classes of $R$.
  Suppose that the underlying morphism of commutative $C$-global ring spectra
  $u_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}(i)$ is a $C$-global localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^{\wedge}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}})$.
  Then $i$ is an ultra-commutative $C$-global localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{URing}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$.
  If this all works out as expected, the localization property of 
  $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow {\mathbf{KR}}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}})$
  from Theorem \ref{thm:Realglobal}
  implies that this morphism is also an ultra-commutative $C$-global localization in $\operatorname{URing}_{C\operatorname{\!\text{-}gl}}$
  by the classes $\tilde b_1$ and $\{b_m\}_{m\geq 2}$.
<!-- end rk-10 -->
<!-- defn-8: body_md -->
Let ${\mathcal M}^\otimes$ be a symmetric monoidal model category
  with cofibrant unit object. A {\em monoidal localization}
  is a lax symmetric monoidal functor
  \[ \gamma^\otimes_{\mathcal M}\ \colon \ N({\mathcal M}^\otimes) \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal M}^\otimes_\infty \]
  to a symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category ${\mathcal M}^\otimes_\infty$
  with the following universal property: for every symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category ${\mathcal D}$,
  the restriction functor
  \[ 
    \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}(\gamma^\otimes_{\mathcal M},{\mathcal D})\ \colon \
    \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}({\mathcal M}^\otimes_\infty,{\mathcal D})\ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}^W(N({\mathcal M}^\otimes),{\mathcal D})
  \]
  is an equivalence of $\infty$-categories. Here the target
  $\operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}^W(N({\mathcal M}^\otimes),{\mathcal D})$ is the full subcategory of
  $\operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}(N({\mathcal M}^\otimes),{\mathcal D})$ spanned by those lax symmetric monoidal
  functors whose underlying functors invert weak equivalences.
<!-- end defn-8 -->
<!-- rk-11: body_md -->
\label{rk:monloc_addendum}
  Clearly, monoidal localizations are unique (in the sense of higher category theory)
  whenever they exist. And Nikolaus and Scholze show in \cite[Theorem A.7]{nikolaus-scholze:TC}
  that every symmetric monoidal model category admits a monoidal localization.
  In the same theorem, they show moreover that
  the monoidal localization has the following additional properties:
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item The functor of underlying $\infty$-categories
    \[ (\gamma^\otimes_{\mathcal M})_{\langle 1\rangle}\ \colon \ N {\mathcal M} = N({\mathcal M}^\otimes)_{\langle 1\rangle} \ \longrightarrow \ ({\mathcal M}^\otimes_\infty)_{\langle 1\rangle} \]
    is a localization of the 1-category ${\mathcal M}$ at the class of weak equivalences.
  \item Let ${\mathcal M}_{\operatorname{cof}}^\otimes$ denote the full symmetric monoidal subcategory
    of cofibrant objects in ${\mathcal M}^\otimes$. Then the composite
    \[ \gamma^\otimes_{{\mathcal M},\operatorname{cof}}\ : \
      N({\mathcal M}^\otimes_{\operatorname{cof}}) \  \ \xrightarrow{\text{incl}} \ N({\mathcal M}^\otimes) \ \xrightarrow{\gamma^\otimes_{\mathcal M}} \ {\mathcal M}^\otimes_\infty \]
    is strong (as opposed to only lax) symmetric monoidal.
 Since $\gamma^\otimes_{{\mathcal M},\operatorname{cof}}$ is both strong symmetric monoidal
    and essentially surjective on objects, precomposition with it `detects strongness',
    in the following sense:
    let $F\colon {\mathcal M}^\otimes_\infty\longrightarrow{\mathcal D}$ be a lax symmetric monoidal functor
    such that the composite $F\circ\gamma^\otimes_{{\mathcal M},\operatorname{cof}}\colon\allowbreak N({\mathcal M}^\otimes_{\operatorname{cof}})\longrightarrow{\mathcal D}$ is strong (as opposed to only lax) symmetric monoidal.
    Then $F$ is strong symmetric monoidal.
  \item
    For every symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category ${\mathcal D}$,
    restriction along $\gamma^\otimes_{{\mathcal M},\operatorname{cof}}$ is an equivalence of $\infty$-categories
 \[    \operatorname{Fun}_\otimes(\gamma^\otimes_{{\mathcal M},\operatorname{cof}},{\mathcal D})\ \colon \
      \operatorname{Fun}_\otimes({\mathcal M}^\otimes_\infty,{\mathcal D})\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim \ } \
      \operatorname{Fun}_\otimes^W(N({\mathcal M}^\otimes_{\operatorname{cof}}),{\mathcal D})\ .  
 \]
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end rk-11 -->
<!-- construction-16: body_md -->
We write $\operatorname{Sp}_G^O$ for the 1-category of orthogonal $G$-spectra.
  A morphism $f\colon X\longrightarrow Y$ of orthogonal $G$-spectra is a {\em ${\underline \pi}_*$-isomorphism}
  if the induced map of equivariant homotopy groups $\pi_k^H(f)\colon \pi_k^H(X)\longrightarrow\pi_k^H(Y)$
  is an isomorphism for all $k\in{\mathbb Z}$ and all closed subgroups $H$ of $G$.
  Various stable model structures on the category of orthogonal $G$-spectra
  have been established  with ${\underline \pi}_*$-isomorphisms as weak equivalences,
  the first one being due to Mandell--May \cite[III Theorem 4.2]{mandell-may}.
  By \cite[III Proposition 7.5]{mandell-may} the smash product of orthogonal $G$-spectra
  is a Quillen bifunctor for the Mandell--May model structure.
  Since the monoidal unit, the $G$-sphere spectrum ${\mathbb S}_G$,
  is cofibrant in this model structure,
  we are dealing with a symmetric monoidal model category.
  The monoidal localization thus yields a symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category
  \[ {\mathcal S} p^{\wedge}_G \ = \ (\operatorname{Sp}_G^{O,\wedge})_\infty \]
  and a lax symmetric monoidal functor
  \[ \gamma_G^\wedge \ : \operatorname{Sp}_G^{O,\wedge}\ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S} p^{\wedge}_G \]
  whose underlying functor
  \[ \gamma_G = (\gamma_G^\wedge)_{\langle 1\rangle}\ : \
    \operatorname{Sp}_G^O \ \longrightarrow \ ({\mathcal S} p_G^{\wedge})_{\langle 1\rangle} = {\mathcal S} p_G \]
  is a localization of the 1-category of orthogonal $G$-spectra
  at the class of ${\underline \pi}_*$-isomorphisms.
  We refer to the underlying $\infty$-category ${\mathcal S} p_G$
  as the {\em $\infty$-category of genuine $G$-spectra}, and to the monoidal structure as the
  {\em equivariant smash product}.
<!-- end construction-16 -->
<!-- construction-17: body_md -->
\label{con:geom_fix}
  We let ${\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge$ denote the presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category
  of based $G$-spaces, defined as the monoidal localization of
  the symmetric monoidal model category $G{\mathbf T}_*$
  of based compactly generated topological $G$-spaces \cite[Proposition B.7]{schwede:global},
  with weak equivalences those morphisms that induce weak homotopy equivalences
  of fixed points for all closed subgroups of $G$. The monoidal structure is by smash product.

  The 1-categorical suspension spectrum  functor
  \[ \Sigma^\infty\ : \ G{\mathbf T}_\ast \ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{Sp}^O_G \]
  from based $G$-spaces to orthogonal $G$-spectra is strong symmetric monoidal
  and a left Quillen functor for the model structure presently under consideration.
  So it descends to a symmetric monoidal left adjoint
  \[ \Sigma^\infty\ : \ {\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge \]
  of presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-categories.
  Gepner--Meier \cite[Corollary C.7]{gepner-meier:equivariantTMF}
  and Clausen--Mathew--Naumann--Noel
  \cite[Theorem A.2]{clausen-mathew-naumann-noel:descent-vanishing}
  show that the suspension spectrum functor
  $\Sigma^\infty\colon {\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge$
  is the universal example of a strong symmetric monoidal left adjoint
  that inverts all representation spheres.
  More precisely,  $\Sigma^\infty\colon {\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge$
  is initial in the full subcategory of ${\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge\backslash \operatorname{CAlg}(\Pr^L)$ spanned
  by those symmetric monoidal left adjoints $F\colon {\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge\longrightarrow {\mathcal D}$ with
  the property that $F(S^V)$ is invertible in ${\mathcal D}$ for every orthogonal $G$-representation $V$.
  
  The 1-categorical fixed point functor
  \[ (-)^G\ : \ G{\mathbf T}_\ast \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathbf T}_* \]
  from based $G$-spaces to based spaces is fully homotopical,
  preserves pushouts and filtered colimits along closed embeddings,
  and commutes with geometric realization and smash products,
  compare \cite[Proposition B.1]{schwede:global}.
  So it descends to a symmetric monoidal left adjoint
  \[ (-)^G\ : \ {\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S}_*^\wedge \]
  on the level of presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-categories.
  Then the composite
  \[  {\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge \ \xrightarrow{(-)^G} \ {\mathcal S}_*^\wedge \ \xrightarrow{\Sigma^\infty}\ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge \]
  is another strong symmetric monoidal left adjoint. For every $G$-representation
  $V$, the space $(S^V)^G$ is a sphere, and thus becomes invertible in ${\mathcal S} p^\wedge$.
  So by the above universal property of ${\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge$ of inverting representation spheres,
  there is a unique strong symmetric monoidal left adjoint
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_Phi^G}
    \Phi^G\ : \ {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge \ ,    
  \end{equation}
  the {\em geometric fixed point functor}, equipped with a homotopy
  that witnesses the commutativity of the following square in $\operatorname{CAlg}(\Pr^L)$:
  \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\label{eq:Phi^G_def_square}
   \xymatrix{
      {\mathcal S}^\wedge_{G,\ast} \ar[r]^-{(-)^G}\ar[d]_{\Sigma^\infty} & {\mathcal S}_*^\wedge\ar[d]^{\Sigma^\infty} \\
      {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge \ar[r]_-{\Phi^G} & {\mathcal S} p^\wedge}        
    \end{aligned} \end{equation}
<!-- end construction-17 -->
<!-- rk-12: body_md -->
Mathew, Naumann and Noel introduce the geometric fixed point functor $\Phi^G$
  somewhat differently in \cite[Definition 6.12]{mathew-naumann-noel:nilpotence},
  as the composite of smashing with $\tilde E {\mathcal P}$, followed by
  the `categorical fixed point' functor $(-)^G\colon {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p^\wedge$,
  right adjoint to the inflation functor $i_G\colon {\mathcal S} p^\wedge\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge$,
  see \eqref{eq:inflation_functor}.
  Here $E{\mathcal P}$ denotes a universal $G$-space for the family of proper closed
  subgroups, and $\tilde E{\mathcal P}$ its unreduced suspension.
  Their geometric fixed point functor is also a strong monoidal left adjoint,
  and it also makes the diagram \eqref{eq:Phi^G_def_square} commute.
  So the two constructions are equivalent by the universal property
  of $\Sigma^\infty\colon {\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}^\wedge\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge$.
<!-- end rk-12 -->
<!-- construction-18: body_md -->
The symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category of spectra is initial
  in the $\infty$-category $\operatorname{CAlg}(\Pr^L_{\operatorname{st}})$ of presentably symmetric monoidal
  stable $\infty$-categories, see \cite[Corollary 4.8.2.19]{lurie:higher_algebra}.
  So there is a unique strong symmetric monoidal left adjoint
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:inflation_functor}
    i_G \ \colon \ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G\ ,   
  \end{equation}
  called the {\em inflation functor}.
  The composite of inflation and geometric fixed points \eqref{eq:define_Phi^G} is a 
  strong symmetric monoidal left adjoint endofunctor of ${\mathcal S} p^\wedge$;
  by virtue of ${\mathcal S} p^\wedge$ being initial in $\operatorname{CAlg}(\Pr^L_{\operatorname{st}})$,
  the composite is uniquely monoidally equivalent to the identity:
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi_p_G}
    \operatorname{Id}_{{\mathcal S} p^\wedge}\ \sim\   \Phi^G\circ i_G\ .
  \end{equation}
<!-- end construction-18 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:Phi_mon_loc}
  For every symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category ${\mathcal D}$, the functors
\[
 \xymatrix{
    \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}(\Phi^G,{\mathcal D})\colon       \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge,{\mathcal D})\ \ar@<.4ex>[r]
      &\ \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}^{\tilde E{\mathcal P}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G,{\mathcal D})\colon \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}(i_G,{\mathcal D}) \ar@<.4ex>[l]  }  \]
  are mutually inverse equivalences of $\infty$-categories, and
  the functors
\[
 \xymatrix{
    \operatorname{Fun}_{\otimes}(\Phi^G,{\mathcal D})\colon  \operatorname{Fun}_{\otimes}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge,{\mathcal D})\ \ar@<.4ex>[r]
      &\ \operatorname{Fun}_{\otimes}^{\tilde E{\mathcal P}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G,{\mathcal D})\colon \operatorname{Fun}_{\otimes}(i_G,{\mathcal D}) \ar@<.4ex>[l]  }  \]
are mutually inverse equivalences of $\infty$-categories.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The morphism of based $G$-spaces $\tilde E{\mathcal P}\wedge i\colon \tilde E{\mathcal P}\longrightarrow\tilde E{\mathcal P}\wedge\tilde E{\mathcal P}$
  is an equivalence in ${\mathcal S}_{G,\ast}$, so the induced morphism of suspension
  spectra
  \[ (\Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P})\wedge i\ \colon\
    \Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P}\ \longrightarrow\
    (\Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P})\wedge (\Sigma^\infty\tilde E{\mathcal P})
  \]
  is an equivalence in ${\mathcal S} p_G$; we have implicitly used the strong
  symmetric monoidal structure of the suspension spectrum functor.
  This means that the morphism $\Sigma^\infty i\colon{\mathbb S}_G\longrightarrow\Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P}$
  is an idempotent object in the sense of \cite[Definition 4.8.2.1]{lurie:higher_algebra}.

  As in \cite[Theorem 6.11]{mathew-naumann-noel:nilpotence},
  we write ${\mathcal S} p_G[{\mathcal P}^{-1}]$ for the full subcategory of ${\mathcal S} p_G$
  spanned by those $G$-spectra $X$ such that the morphism 
  $X\wedge i\colon X\longrightarrow X\wedge\tilde E{\mathcal P}$ is an equivalence.
  Because $\Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P}$ is an idempotent algebra,
  this subcategory inherits a unique symmetric monoidal structure,
  denoted ${\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge[{\mathcal P}^{-1}]$, such that the  Bousfield localization functor
  \[ (\Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P})\wedge - \ \colon  \ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G[{\mathcal P}^{-1}] \]
  becomes strong symmetric monoidal, see \cite[Proposition 4.8.2.7]{lurie:higher_algebra}.
  In particular, this functor is a monoidal localization
  by the class of geometric fixed point equivalences, i.e., the functor
  \[  \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}( (\Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P})\wedge - ,{\mathcal D})\colon  \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G[{\mathcal P}^{-1}],{\mathcal D})\ \longrightarrow
    \ \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}^{\tilde E{\mathcal P}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G,{\mathcal D})\]
  is an equivalence.

  Mathew, Naumann and Noel show in \cite[Theorem 6.11]{mathew-naumann-noel:nilpotence}
  that the composite strong symmetric monoidal functor
  \[ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge \ \xrightarrow{\ i_G \ }\ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G \ \xrightarrow{\Sigma^\infty\tilde E{\mathcal P}\wedge-} \
    {\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G[{\mathcal P}^{-1}]  \]
  is an equivalence of symmetric monoidal $\infty$-categories.
  So in the diagram      
  \[
   \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G[{\mathcal P}^{-1}],{\mathcal D})\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}( (\Sigma^\infty \tilde E{\mathcal P})\wedge - ,{\mathcal D})} 
    \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}^{\tilde E{\mathcal P}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G,{\mathcal D})
   \xrightarrow{\operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}(i_G,{\mathcal D})} \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge,{\mathcal D})
   \]
the first functor and the composite are equivalences, hence so is the second.
 Since $\Phi^G$ is monoidally left
 inverse to $i_G$ by \eqref{eq:Phi_p_G}, the functor
  \[     \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}(\Phi^G,{\mathcal D})\colon \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge,{\mathcal D})\ \longrightarrow\
    \operatorname{Fun}_{\operatorname{lax}}^{\tilde E{\mathcal P}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G,{\mathcal D})  \]
  is an equivalence of $\infty$-categories, too.
  Since both  $i_G$ and $\Phi^G$ are strong (as opposed to just lax)
  symmetric monoidal, composition with them preserves the full subcategories
  $\operatorname{Fun}_{\otimes}^{\tilde E{\mathcal P}}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G,{\mathcal D})$ and $\operatorname{Fun}_{\otimes}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge,{\mathcal D})$,
  so the restrictions to these full subcategories are equivalences, too.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- construction-19: body_md -->
\label{con:geomfix}
  We let $G$ be a compact Lie group, $X$ an orthogonal $G$-spectrum,
  and $k\in{\mathbb Z}$ an integer. The {\em $k$-th $G$-geometric fixed point group} is
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_geom_fix}
  \Phi_k^G(X)\ = \ \operatorname{colim}_{m+k\geq 0, V\in s({\mathcal U}_G)} [S^{V^G\oplus {\mathbb R}^{m+k}},X(V\oplus {\mathbb R}^m)^G] \ .  
  \end{equation}
  Here $s({\mathcal U}_G)$ is the poset, under inclusion, of finite-dimensional
  $G$-subrepresentations of the complete $G$-universe ${\mathcal U}_G$.
  And `$m+k\geq 0$' means that $m$ runs over the poset of those natural numbers
  such that $m+k$ is non-negative.
  For $m\leq n$ and $V\leq W$ in $s({\mathcal U}_G)$, the transition maps
  $[S^{V^G\oplus {\mathbb R}^{m+k}},X(V\oplus{\mathbb R}^m)^G]\longrightarrow [S^{W^G\oplus{\mathbb R}^{n+k}},X(W\oplus{\mathbb R}^n)^G]$
  in the colimit system generalize those in
  \cite[Definition 3.3.1]{schwede:global}.
  The monoidal natural isomorphism \eqref{eq:Phi_vs_Phi} below
  gives a different perspective on these 
  geometric fixed point groups, namely as the homotopy groups of
  a geometric fixed point spectrum $\Phi^G(X)$.
    
  The geometric fixed point groups are multiplicative, in the following sense.
  For orthogonal $G$-spectra $X$ and $Y$, we define external multiplication maps
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:cdot_Phi^G}
    \times\ : \ \Phi_k^G(X)\times \Phi_l^G(Y)\ \longrightarrow \ \Phi_{k+l}^G(X\wedge Y)\ .     
  \end{equation}
  We let $f\colon S^{V^G\oplus{\mathbb R}^{m+k}}\longrightarrow X(V\oplus{\mathbb R}^m)^G$ and
  $g\colon S^{W^G\oplus{\mathbb R}^{n+l}}\longrightarrow Y(W\oplus{\mathbb R}^n)^G$
  be continuous based maps that represent classes $x=[f]\in \Phi_k^G(X)$ and $y=[g]\in\Phi_l^G(Y)$,
  respectively. We define $x\times y$ as the class represented by
  the following composite:
  \begin{align*}
    S^{(V\oplus W)^G\oplus {\mathbb R}^{m+n+k+l}}\
    &\xrightarrow{\text{shuffle}}\
    S^{V^G\oplus {\mathbb R}^{m+k}\oplus  W^G\oplus{\mathbb R}^{n+l}}\\
    &\xrightarrow{f\wedge g}\ X(V\oplus{\mathbb R}^m)^G\wedge Y(W\oplus{\mathbb R}^n)^G\ = \ (X(V\oplus{\mathbb R}^m)\wedge Y(W\oplus{\mathbb R}^n))^G\\
    &\xrightarrow{(\iota_{V\oplus{\mathbb R}^m,W\oplus{\mathbb R}^n})^G} \ ((X\wedge Y)(V\oplus{\mathbb R}^m\oplus W\oplus{\mathbb R}^n))^G \\
    &\xrightarrow{\text{shuffle}}\ ((X\wedge Y)( V\oplus W\oplus{\mathbb R}^{m+n}))^G 
  \end{align*}
  Here $\iota_{V\oplus{\mathbb R}^m,W\oplus{\mathbb R}^n}$ is a component of the universal bimorphism.

  Essentially the same arguments as for the pairing on equivariant homotopy groups
  in \cite[Theorem 3.5.14]{schwede:global} show that the pairing
  \eqref{eq:cdot_Phi^G} is biadditive, unital, associative and commutative,
  the latter with respect to the Koszul sign $(-1)^{k l}$ on pairs of elements
  of degree $(k,l)$. We omit the formal proof.
<!-- end construction-19 -->
<!-- construction-20: body_md -->
\label{con:descend_pi_and_Phi}
  The universal property of the monoidal localization functor 
  $\gamma^\wedge_G\colon\operatorname{Sp}^{O,\wedge}_G\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G$ allows us to descend
  the multiplicative structure of the homotopy group functors $\pi_*^G$
  and the geometric fixed point functors $\Phi^G_*$ from the orthogonal spectrum model
  to the $\infty$-category of $G$-spectra, as follows.

  We write $\operatorname{GrAb}^\otimes$ for the symmetric monoidal 1-category of
  ${\mathbb Z}$-graded abelian groups, under graded tensor product, 
  and with the Koszul sign built into the symmetry isomorphism.
  We write $\pi_*^G(X)=\{\pi_k^G(X)\}_{k\in{\mathbb Z}}$ for the ${\mathbb Z}$-graded $G$-equivariant
  homotopy groups of an orthogonal $G$-spectrum $X$.
  By \cite[Theorem 3.5.14]{schwede:global}, the maps
  \[ \times \ \colon \ \pi_k^G(X)\times\pi_l^G(Y)\ \longrightarrow \ \pi_{k+l}^G(X\wedge Y) \]
  defined in \cite[(3.5.13)]{schwede:global}
  endow the functor $\pi_*^G$ with a lax symmetric monoidal structure.
  By definition, this functor also inverts ${\underline \pi}_*$-isomorphisms,
  so it descends uniquely through
  the monoidal localization $\gamma^\wedge_G\colon\operatorname{Sp}^{O,\wedge}_G\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G$.
  In other words, there is a unique lax symmetric monoidal functor
  \[ \bar\pi_*^G \ \colon\  {\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G \ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{GrAb}^\otimes \]
  equipped with a monoidal natural isomorphism
  \[  \bar\pi_*^G\circ \gamma^\wedge_G \ \cong \ \pi_*^G   \]
  between lax symmetric monoidal functors $\operatorname{Sp}^{O,\wedge}_G\longrightarrow\operatorname{GrAb}^\otimes$.
  
  Similarly, the maps \eqref{eq:cdot_Phi^G} endow the functor $\Phi_*^G$
  with a lax symmetric monoidal structure.
  This functor inverts ${\underline \pi}_*$-isomorphisms by \cite[Proposition 3.3.10]{schwede:global},
  so it, too,  descends uniquely through
  the monoidal localization $\gamma^\wedge_G\colon\operatorname{Sp}^{O,\wedge}_G\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G$:
  there is a unique lax symmetric monoidal functor
  \[ \bar\Phi_*^G \ \colon\ {\mathcal S} p^\wedge_G \ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{GrAb}^\otimes \]
  equipped with a monoidal natural isomorphism
    \[
  \bar\Phi_*^G\circ \gamma^\wedge_G \ \cong \ \Phi_*^G\ .    
\]
  The {\em geometric fixed point homomorphism}
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_Phi^G_map}
    \Phi^G\ \colon\ \pi_k^G(X)\ \longrightarrow\  \Phi^G_k(X)
  \end{equation}
  does what the name suggests:
  it sends the class of a $G$-map $f\colon S^{U\oplus{\mathbb R}^{m+k}}\longrightarrow X(U\oplus{\mathbb R}^m)$
  to the class of the map
